item.description: The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO on how to extract value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has long rewarded.
item.content:encoded:
The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO on how to extract value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has long rewarded.

Not a generic Silicon Valley critique but a specific investigation with course names, dollar figures and named people; if you care about early-stage investing and talent pipelines, the detail density is high.

5:12 You can raise hundreds of thousands before you have a company
Pre-idea funding was the newest layer of the game when Theo arrived on campus: give an 18-year-old who just started school hundreds of thousands, even millions, of dollars, sign a one-page SAFE check, agree that "when you start a company someday, come back to us" — otherwise the money never has to be repaid. For a VC that's pocket change; they don't really believe in these hyped-up teenagers, and they don't need you personally to succeed — they just need one to blow up overnight. Meanwhile students are encouraged to make enormous promises and then discover again and again that no one follows up: lie, and nothing happens.

13:22 The secret course teaches extracting value
Stanford has a course that isn't in the catalog, called How to Rule the World, taught by a Silicon Valley CEO who packages himself as a professor, admitting only 12 students a year — merely knowing it exists is a status symbol. Its central assignment is extracting value from people, with a strong whiff of the ends justifying the means. One woman Theo interviewed said the course taught her how to lie to VCs to raise money — she later actually raised millions and dropped out of Stanford, despite having already been caught cheating in a computer science class; months later she put out a glossy launch video for a technology that didn't exist, and Silicon Valley applauded anyway, she moved into a mansion, and she was invited back to Stanford to give a talk.

26:46 Ethics isn't a premise; getting caught is what counts
During ethics week in the intro computer science course, the professor discussed a case where a software defect killed four people in a radiotherapy device, and the TA asked who in the room cared about ethics — Theo was the only one who raised his hand. Weeks later a classmate told him he was taking a business ethics course, and "we're all just there to figure out how they got caught." He didn't sense that these people felt any need to pretend to care; when Sam Bankman-Fried was under house arrest at the house on the Stanford campus where he grew up, students made pilgrimages, threw parties themed around him, and said they wanted to replicate his success minus the final fall. A colleague's summary of the money that mysteriously vanished at Tree Hacks: it's all just a little bit of fraud.

38:01 The real reason the president fell wasn't the data
Board members who ousted Marc Tessier-Lavigne later told Theo that one of the heaviest reasons they gave was his posture — a highly aggressive public stance when challenged, deny, deny, deny, plus the threatening letters sent by the lawyer he hired, Steve Neal, which embarrassed the university. Theo found no evidence that Tessier-Lavigne himself falsified data: the problem was in the labs he oversaw, where subordinates committed fraud in papers he co-authored, including the 2009 paper claiming to have found the cause of Alzheimer's, while internal company results before publication showed its central finding was "at best unreliable." He was asked to retract and refused, dragging it out for a decade. What drove him out was image management, not the data.

39:01 Four days after being ousted, the mansion deal closed
Four days after the board unanimously removed him, Tessier-Lavigne closed on a 7,600-square-foot mansion in "America's most expensive zip code," valued at over $10 million; eight months later he announced he had raised $1 billion for a new company doing AI biotech. Of the two VCs that led the round, an investor at one messaged Theo two months later to rib him, followed by a winking emoji; an investor at the other offered him money to start a company. Theo says it's the most Silicon Valley thing you could imagine: everything can be monetized, even taking down a university president turns into an invitation.

45:44 Duck syndrome: paddling like mad under the surface
Duck syndrome is a term Stanford coined itself: students glide across the surface like ducks, making everything look effortless, while underneath their legs paddle desperately just to stay afloat. Katie Meyer was its best illustration — women's soccer captain, led the team to an NCAA title, headed to law school, didn't drink, didn't smoke, didn't speed. Months before graduation, late on a Friday night, after every student support office had closed, she received a letter: because six months earlier she had spilled coffee on a football player (she said it was an accident, he said it was deliberate), her degree was suspended. That night she took her own life. Twelve schools later paid tribute to her; Stanford was not among them. The women's soccer team she had just captained held a mental health night and didn't mention her name.

52:01 A legendary professor's fraud case, and the school says it never heard of it
Stan Cohen was the first geneticist to transplant a gene from one living organism into another, and his 1970s recombinant DNA technique gave rise to the model of universities making money from patents; in its final valid year that patent contributed 62% of all of Stanford's patent revenue. In his freshman year Theo found that Cohen had been found by a court to have committed fraud: he promised investors a drug target that might cure Huntington's disease and said the drug was already approved to treat another condition, without telling them it had been permanently banned by the FDA in 1976 because it was lethal. He was ultimately ordered to pay $29 million and paid it. Theo asked the university, and the university replied that it had never heard of the case and had no involvement whatsoever — even though Stanford owned the relevant intellectual property and had been subpoenaed by the court.

55:04 Raising money is easier than an internship, and that itself is a signal
The saying circulating in Stanford's inner circles is that raising money for a startup is easier than getting an internship — Theo says that's absurd, it shouldn't be that way, but that's the reality. He describes the moment as a game of AI musical chairs: everyone is waiting to see who's still standing when the music stops and who's left holding the bag. He isn't worried about cash-flow-positive companies like Meta and Google; he's worried about the companies clinging to the AI narrative that have no technology of their own, no revenue, and no ability to generate revenue — they can't hold on, and they will collapse. But he also cautions that Silicon Valley hasn't held power for long; it's a very immature power system that hasn't grown guardrails, transparency or accountability, and one collapse doesn't necessarily mean a reckoning.

item.title: America's Manufacturing Hollow-Out Isn't a Capability Problem, It's a Financial-Return Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.description: Chris Power says the US manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement while China manages it like national security; tariffs are only an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Power says the US manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement while China manages it like national security; tariffs are only an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing rivals' industrial capacity.

Two frontline hardware founders lay out the real bottlenecks of American reindustrialization: not technology, but trust, cost, and how you define a supply chain. High information density, and the back half on tariffs and subsidies is the most valuable part.

2:02 The reserve currency is the first step of decline
Chris Power gives a four-step cycle: a great power first has a generative population and the best industrial capacity, then wins or prevents a war, then becomes extremely lazy, and finally outsources the very things that made it successful. He says this cycle repeats roughly every 150 years — the Dutch gave way to the British, the British gave way to the Americans — and each time industrial power is re-traded for financial power, the world's reserve currency changes hands. That judgment is the starting point for his founding Hadrian: you think you're Mike Tyson at his peak, and your opponent thinks you're the Mike Tyson right before Buster Douglas knocked him out.

9:10 90% of the factory is a software problem
Chris Power says the biggest misconception about advanced manufacturing is that when people see someone moving things in a factory, they assume it's a humanoid robot problem. In reality, 90% of advanced manufacturing is smart people sitting at computers doing digital engineering, or operating an extremely dumb computer on the shop floor. A welder or machinist has to stand in front of the machine because the system isn't closed-loop — they're doing trigonometry in their heads, judging whether the tool is about to snap. That's why Hadrian positions itself as a software company: it breaks physical tasks into high-judgment fixturing, then hands execution to robots, CNCs, or welding systems.

14:14 Software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in LA
Tom Mueller says Southern California's aerospace talent ecosystem is recovering — three or four years after SpaceX was founded in 2002, the aerospace employment curve in the South Bay started turning up. He lists what this area is doing simultaneously: nuclear companies, drone companies, defense companies, 3D printing companies, plus Anduril in Orange County. The two companies poach from each other and compete for talent, and Northrop Grumman is right across the street from Impulse. Tom's summary: software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware is done in LA.

15:17 Vertical integration is for learning the problem, not saving money
Tom Mueller explains the real logic of SpaceX-style vertical integration: you have to build the first development engine or spacecraft yourself, because in the prototype phase you need to learn every assembly and machining problem. If you hand it to a machine shop from the start, the drawing has problems, the parts come back and don't fit, and you learn nothing. Once the design converges, then you outsource. Chris Power adds that every company should keep 10% to 15% of in-house capacity, because there's always a "hot pot" moment when you need a genius to make something within an hour to hit a flight milestone — but scale has to happen outside.

16:18 Outsourcing decisions run on trust, not finance
Chris Power says what's bought and sold in manufacturing is trust. Hadrian's vertical integration strategy is to outsource as much as possible to every reindustrialization startup and small business, because there are too many projects to run. But they will vertically integrate the links where they "don't believe you can deliver on time" — that's not a financial trade-off, it's a willingness to spend an extra two million dollars on equipment and hire a team rather than bet risk on a legacy foundry that has been late on every submarine program for the past thirty years. His exact words: most of America is incompetent at trust and scheduling.

19:20 In World War II, America was China
Chris Power uses World War II as an analogy: German engineers crushed America on engineering, but America ground them down with McDonald's-style mass production and better logistics. He says America played the role in World War II that China plays today — not by engineering best, but by producing most. Now the situation is reversed: US missile stockpiles run out in seven days in war games, and China built 2,600 ships while America built six. His conclusion: you can have the best Raytheon missile, but if you can't mass-produce it, you have no options.

21:23 The robot bottleneck is the velocity of training data
Chris Power says the robotics race ultimately comes down to software, and software — especially AI — now comes down to the velocity of training data, which in turn depends on physical-world deployment, meaning mass manufacturing. So this isn't a friendly competition between American companies over "whether Tesla sells a few more Optimus units or Google wins" — it's a civilizational-level confrontation. Tom Mueller adds from the space angle: building on the Moon and Mars requires robot legions rather than humans, because the environment is too dangerous and too expensive; a good robot needs three things — dexterous hands, vision that's basically solved, and an AI brain.

29:40 Tariffs are an imperfect corrective tool
Chris Power says manufacturing has four inputs: energy, labor, cost of capital, and export tariffs. He has run the numbers: even if you set Hadrian's labor cost and energy cost to zero, imported components from China are still three times cheaper than buying raw materials in America and making them yourself. He argues China has run industrial policy as national security since 1985, subsidizing energy, labor, capital, and export tariffs, while America manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial-statement returns. The problem with tariffs is enforcement: ban China but not Singapore, and Chinese companies route through Singapore; differences in the definition of raw materials and assembly also end up hurting American firms that import components from Mexico.

item.title: He Cooked the Chickpea Pasta Into Mush, Then Survived by Telling People to Steep It Like Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.description: Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board — 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said ‘steep it like tea’ and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.
item.content:encoded:
Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board — 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said ‘steep it like tea’ and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.

The founder's account is dense with failure detail: three scrapped production batches, a kidney stone, being thrown out of the factory, a 30% week-over-week decline. Worth hearing for anyone who wants to know how you survive a near-death moment.

5:14 The starting point wasn't a business insight, it was a runny nose
In college Brian's fridge held nothing but hummus, eating was just ‘fuel’ to him, and he cycled between antibiotics and steroids for so long he was nearly facing surgery. It was his father, an orthodontist, who got him to try an elimination diet, and that's how he found that wheat-based foods triggered sinus inflammation — one beer and the next day he couldn't breathe. The ENT told him: I don't know what you're talking about, but if it works, keep doing it. That private problem later became the product definition: high-protein, high-fiber, gluten-free pasta, doing what Chobani did for yogurt.

10:26 The first recipe had chia in it and was too sticky to look at
He bought Bob's Red Mill chickpea flour on Amazon and followed blogs for combinations. The first version was chickpeas plus eggs plus chia — the chia made it so sticky the result was ugly. With no rolling pin he used a wine bottle; with no pasta cutter he used a knife, dusting flour on the table as he cut to keep it from sticking. The second version dropped the chia, leaving just chickpeas and eggs, and was clearly better, but to make it usable for more people he added tapioca starch and xanthan gum back in and committed to the vegan route. His first capital expenditure was an Atlas Mercado hand-crank pasta machine, about $30 on Amazon. He got up at 5 a.m. every day to make pasta, put on country music, and his roommates thought he was insane.

20:49 Going from 200 pounds an hour to 1,000 magnified every mistake
They first found a tiny gluten-free factory in Michigan that could only do 150 to 200 pounds an hour — wildly inefficient, but they could learn as they went. To get into 190 Meijer stores and 2 Eataly locations, that capacity wasn't enough, so they found what was then the largest gluten-free pasta factory in the country, outside Los Angeles. The problem: that plant had only ever run rice and corn pasta, never legumes. After scaling to roughly 1,000 pounds an hour, the pasta coming out looked fine but turned into total mush the moment you boiled it. Each trial run was 8,000 to 10,000 pounds, and a failure meant the die costs and ingredient costs were all gone — and they had only a little over $100,000 on hand.

26:02 He got thrown out of the factory for asking the operator
After several failed trial runs, Brian ignored the other side's objections and went straight to the line operator to ask what was actually going wrong. The worker said ‘this corn smells weird,’ and he answered: that's not corn, we're not making corn pasta today, it's chickpeas. He realized on the spot that communication had broken down completely, and right after that he was escorted out of the plant. At the same time the distributor was threatening him: if you don't fulfill this purchase order, you'll never work with this retailer again. He later estimated this shipment would cost nearly every dollar they had.

28:07 The fix was don't boil it — steep it like tea
With nowhere left to turn they started testing: boil one minute, two minutes, three minutes, then just stop boiling altogether — bring water to a boil, turn off the heat, and let the pasta sit in the hot water. What came out of steeping was better than what came out of boiling, or at least it didn't fall apart. Brian says he wasn't proud of the product, and it bothered him to sell it under his own brand, but he knew it was a life-or-death question. The packaging was already printed, so they could only make extra stickers reading ‘Banza is easier to cook than regular pasta — steep it like tea,’ and then find people to hand-apply them to 20,000 boxes. Once that shipment went out, they immediately pulled out of the big factory and went back to the small one in Michigan.

35:18 The box is orange because every other pasta box is blue
They noticed that nearly every pasta package on the shelf at the time was blue — Brian put it as ‘you'd think they'd colluded.’ Orange contrasts most strongly with blue, and orange was also the color he'd loved since watching Nickelodeon as a kid, so it became the brand color. The packaging copy involved trade-offs too: putting ‘chickpeas’ in the most prominent spot would scare off a lot of people, and so would gluten-free, so the gluten-free certification went on the side while the front led with high protein and high fiber — making consumers feel this was ‘a product for me’ rather than ‘not a product for me.’

41:31 The glyphosate report cut weekly sales by a third
Moms Across America published a report claiming glyphosate residue was detected in Banza products. Brian saw the Google alert during a one-on-one meeting; he says his heart sank and his mind jumped twenty steps ahead. He wanted to verify first, so he only issued a statement saying ‘we are investigating’ — which was nowhere near enough for the most panicked people. The lab results were delayed again and again, dragging on for three weeks. The final published result was 98% below the allegation, but not zero — still a very low level, and below the EWG's risk benchmark. He decided to make the supply chain 100% traceable and to join the Detox Project's certification program.

52:15 The natural channel recovered far more slowly than conventional
The sales recovery was a mixed bag: some channels came back better than before, but the natural channel recovered much more slowly — and that was exactly the customer base with the best repeat purchase rates and the highest sales per store. Brian says this actually makes sense, because natural-channel consumers are the most susceptible to this kind of information. What he does now: he keeps alerts on for anywhere Banza and glyphosate are mentioned, and personally goes on Reddit to reply and add context, with the goal of making it impossible for the story to be seen without its context. He also admits he should have acknowledged what was happening faster and more visibly at the time.

item.title: AI Won't Replace People — What Replaces Them Is the Work Nobody Wrote Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.description: Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of its own workflows — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own models.
item.content:encoded:
Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of its own workflows — that "map of work" is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own models.

Daniel Dines breaks down the real bottleneck of AI landing inside enterprises from UiPath's front-line view, with a high density of counter-consensus claims — suited to anyone trying to judge the pace of enterprise AI adoption.

6:17 AI does not change its own weights on the job
Daniel argues the biggest difference between AI and humans is not reasoning ability, but that AI does not change its own weights on the job. A human is changed by a job; AI just writes things into a notebook. He gives the example of two chefs: one who has cooked Japanese cuisine for 20 years, one who has cooked Italian for 20 years — give them the same recipe and what they produce is completely different. This is not something you can replicate by writing the company down on paper, because human judgment comes from years of being reshaped by the work. So on the claim that "there are millions of Einsteins in the data center," Daniel thinks what Dario meant is millions of entities with partial reasoning ability, not Einsteins who can learn on the job the way a person does.

16:29 Probabilistic tech should not do work that demands precision
Daniel raises another limit on AI: precision. Every step AI takes is probabilistic — even if each step is 99% correct, after 100 steps the overall success rate may be down to 60%. So make AI do long multiplication repeatedly and it will eventually get it wrong. His conclusion: the fact that a tool can do something does not mean you should use it for that thing. ChatGPT looks like it is doing arithmetic, but behind the scenes it is calling a computer tool — the precision is not coming from ChatGPT. Extend that logic to the enterprise level: all work that demands precision should run on precise technology; there is no reason for it to run on probabilistic technology.

18:34 Deploying AI hasn't gotten easier; deploying automation has
Daniel points to an asymmetry inside enterprises: deploying AI agents is no easier than it was two years ago, but deploying automation has become much easier, because you can use coding agents to generate the automation. He lists ChatGPT, chain of thoughts and coding agents as the three main milestones. Coding agents work at "design time"; people use them to build automations that run precisely every time at "execution time"; and when an automation breaks because an upstream system changed, AI can come back and fix it. The result is that AI is generating the software that runs the company, and that software cannot change its behavior in real time — it can be audited, tested and read by people. This is the pattern he sees taking shape in enterprises right now.

23:46 Blind layoffs cut the people AI most needs
In his book Daniel puts forward the concept of the "credentialed middle": companies used to hire people on the basis of deep domain credentials, and that is exactly the kind of expertise AI helps with most. His judgment is counterintuitive — you will be inclined to cut the people who are not the biggest experts in the domain, but those are precisely the people you will need to supplement AI into expert work. He gives the example of a law firm: it used to hire 25 interns a year, this year it hired only 4. He agrees most roles will need fewer people, but the key question is "which people." His criterion: keep the ones with the most initiative, who can maintain client relationships, who can mentor newcomers, who carry the company culture — because AI cannot show initiative in the human sense.

25:51 What decides whether AI can take over is how clear the framework is
Harry argues finance and accounting work is highly verifiable and therefore easy for AI to replace. Daniel disagrees outright: it is not a question of verifiability, but of whether the work is framed by a framework someone else has already defined. He says finance is precisely an area where the framework is unclear — receive an invoice or an order and there can be different ways to handle it, such as whether Nvidia would ship to OpenAI first, and that rule may never have been written down at all. If the rules are not captured by a framework, AI cannot learn them. So a company must first hand the "map of work" to AI: all workflows, all exceptions, all processes, all systems. This is also what he keeps stressing: models are interchangeable; the map of work and the processes around it are where the real value lies.

29:01 Use agents to interview employees and draw the work as a map
UiPath has launched a technology called cartography, as a discipline that helps companies surface how work actually gets done. Concretely, it uses a product called a cartographer agent to interview real business experts and have them record what they are doing, with the agent following up in real time: why did you change how you handled this invoice because the zip code was different? Why did you take another path? That is how exceptions get dug out one by one. Then the data from multiple people is aggregated to generate a real-time process map. With that "map of work" in hand, you use coding agents to design how the process should be transformed, and ultimately, through "printing software," push the process from purely manual point A toward a state with fewer people operating systems and more automation and agentic AI operating systems.

34:15 Vibe coding is easy for prototypes, hard for production
Daniel admits UiPath tried vibe coding; at first it looked astonishingly effective, but pushing it into production hit a wall: connectors, permissions, auditing, security — all of it has to be maintained. He gives his own example of writing a procurement tool: initially written entirely by AI, but the database schema was completely wrong and someone had to rebuild the structure. His conclusion is that going from prototype to production is where the real work is, not writing the code itself. In the end you will likely pay as much as, or more than, the tool you replaced, while also consuming the bandwidth of your best people. So he does not think systems of record like Salesforce will be replaced by vibe coding.

45:34 The opportunity in legal AI is in the process, not the model call
Harry does the math: the US legal industry is a $300 billion market, and if 30% of the labor can be replaced that is $90 billion in revenue. Daniel counters that the $90 billion will not convert into token revenue — maybe only 10%, so a $10 billion token opportunity. His judgment: for legal opinions, both open-source and frontier models are good enough; what is actually valuable is the custom workflow built around the legal process. If Harvey and Lagora just help you call a model once to get a legal opinion, that will not be a hundred-billion-dollar market; but if they really draw the work as a map, build out the workflows and create a legal department for you, the value is far greater.

item.title: Even Legal-Cannabis States Can't Escape: A Federal Ban Is About to Empty the THC Shelves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.description: A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even legal-cannabis states will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.
item.content:encoded:
A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even legal-cannabis states will feel it when they lose the cheap alternative.

Eight minutes that explain how a regulatory loophole grew into an industry and how it gets cut off in one stroke — for anyone watching policy risk and regulatory arbitrage.

0:00 Legal-cannabis states don't escape a federal ban
Half of US states have legal recreational cannabis, but the reason THC drinks, vapes and gummies can be sold openly in states that ban cannabis is a loophole left by the 2018 farm bill: it allows low-concentration THC from hemp. After lab processing, that low concentration is enough to mimic a cannabis high, which is how you get Delta 8, Delta 9 — and, as the show jokes, by now Delta 11. Congress now wants to close the loophole, and it is using a stricter ban to do it. The key point is that this is a federal ban, so even if your state has legal cannabis, you get hit.

1:00 What's being banned is a $28 billion industry
The show puts the size at $28 billion and says the industry could disappear before the end of this year. Tennessee has already gone first: since July it has banned most THC hemp products, and a local reporter describes herself as already living in a ‘post-hemp world’. State legislators even beat Congress to it, banning full-spectrum CBD and smokable flower first. For retailers, farmers and processors, this isn't a policy debate — it's a choice they have to make before year-end.

3:07 Farmers are going back from hemp to blackberries and corn
Tennessee farmer Lee Crabtree's farm used to grow mostly CBD-variety hemp, and the new state law makes selling those products illegal, so he has gone back to traditional seasonal crops like blackberries and corn. The family still has the industrial kitchen from its CBD food days, and now his wife Stacy uses that big stainless-steel counter to cut grapes for chicken salad and sell it at the roadside farmers market. Lee says income is down, and if the traditional crops don't sell, he'll have to go find a job. This is what the ban looks like landing on one household.

5:08 The regulator's reason: consumers don't know what they're drinking
Tennessee Republican Representative William Lamberth uses a drinks analogy: someone buying a Sprite expects a Sprite, not a beer; someone buying a beer expects a beer, not a tequila; someone buying a tequila expects not to get a Sprite. He says the goal is for consumers to know exactly what they're buying. But even farmers who agree with the logic worry the law goes too far. The show also gives the other side: big companies are laying people off, and some are simply moving states — Emily Schaeferich's company Burning Acre moved from Columbia, Tennessee, to North Carolina to keep growing, and she admits ripping up the entire retail, manufacturing and wholesale supply chain ‘definitely costs a lot of money’.

6:10 Moving to another state may be wasted effort
Hemp economist Beau Whitney calls the nationwide ban taking effect in December an ‘extinction-level event’. His mechanism: cannabis can only be grown in certain states, while hemp can be grown and shipped anywhere, so hemp businesses can build supersized capacity, push costs down and ship nationwide; cannabis, by contrast, needs a separate supply chain per state and can't get hemp's economies of scale. The result is that hemp-derived foods are far cheaper than their cannabis equivalents. So even in states with legal recreational cannabis, consumers will feel the squeeze when they lose the cheap alternative.

7:13 The ban takes out state tax revenue
The show pulls out economies of scale on its own to explain it: the more of the same good you produce, the lower the unit cost, and the savings can be passed on to consumers. That also explains why hemp-derived foods are cheaper than cannabis products. But consumers aren't the only ones affected. For a lot of state budgets, losing the hemp industry means losing a sizable source of tax revenue — in Tennessee alone, a $54 million budget hole. Beau Whitney also says it could put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk.

7:13 The delay just moves it from November to December
The White House has urged Congress to delay or amend the ban, the Senate currently supports it, and the House voted earlier this month to delay it too. But those moves only push the effective date from November to December — a one-month delay. For companies that have already moved states and rebuilt supply chains, a month changes nothing — they may have just moved the whole business only to find the industry destroyed in December.

8:14 Those staying behind switch to fiber hemp
Tennessee farmer Bill Corbin, in Springfield, is preparing the first fiber hemp crop for the French company Hemp-It; this hemp is used for rope, packaging and car parts. He says there isn't a single person in the industry who didn't know this day was coming, and he thinks the industry was unsustainable to begin with, and he agrees with legislators' efforts to suppress recreational use of hemp derivatives. But he worries about medical consumers: he himself is older and has arthritis, relies heavily on full-spectrum CBD, and the products left after the ban may not be strong enough for older people or those trying to avoid opioid painkillers.

item.title: The Bat Doesn't Know What It's Like to Be a Bat Either
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.description: The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.
item.content:encoded:
The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.

The second half of episode 400, and listenable on its own. The first half is about theories of consciousness; the second half drifts unexpectedly into animal ethics, and the four of them never do settle their disagreement.

1:07 A bat having an inner world is not the same as being conscious
Christopher summarises Dennett's response: he flatly denies Nagel — we can talk about what it's like to be a bat in all sorts of ways (by first ruling out the things bats don't do, for instance), and with enough information we eventually get there, because "what it's like to be a bat" just is the discriminative, dispositional states a bat has. Dylan supplies the step Dennett actually rejects: drawing on von Uexküll's Umwelt and Innenwelt (surrounding world and inner world), Dennett grants that a bat has an inner world, which is not crazy; what he won't accept is the move straight from "has an inner world" to "therefore consciousness exists," and that is exactly the move Nagel uses to prove consciousness exists. Our mode of access is heterophenomenology: treat the bat's behaviour and physiology as a text to be explained.

5:37 Consciousness is not an all-or-nothing property
Christopher reads out a passage from Dennett: are language-less animals not conscious at all? Dennett says the question shouldn't be taken as a given challenge, because it presupposes "something we've had a hard time getting rid of" — that consciousness is an all-or-nothing property that splits the universe into two utterly different categories: things that have it and things that don't. That dichotomy is what Dennett wants to dismantle; what he wants is consciousness in degrees. Christopher then offers his own version: he doesn't want to accept property dualism, he wants to deny the hard problem, because subjectivity can perfectly well have a biological and evolutionary explanation — agency and subjectivity co-evolved; a physical process organising itself from the inside so that it "feels like something" is a real biological phenomenon.

12:57 The bat doesn't know what it's like to be a bat either
Seth pushes the argument to its extreme: it isn't "we don't know what it's like to be a bat," it's that there is no "what it's like to be a bat as seen from the bat's side" at all; the bat doesn't know either, because it lacks the machinery to string experiences into a narrative and give them names. Dylan immediately marks the cost of this inference: if anything with dynamic activity has its own experience, then atoms count too, and that's panpsychism. Christopher says you don't have to go all the way to atoms, but concedes the direction does sound like panpsychism — he'd rather use a threshold: you need a feedback loop of perception and action before you can talk about a new way of being.

14:35 Even plants have a perspective in some sense
Mark digs up a line from Dennett's book: the perspective of a conscious observer is a refined descendant of the original perspective of the first replicators, which "divided the world into good and bad" — on that account even plants have a perspective in this sense, and "perspective" becomes a metaphor. Christopher then offers gradualism: from sponges to mantis shrimp to humans, subjectivity accumulates layer by layer and gets thicker and thicker, with a fuzzy threshold in between. Dylan wants to nail the threshold down harder: you can't use "complex" as the criterion, since weather is a complex self-maintaining system too; the difference is that living things can replicate themselves and have a wholeness, so the only thing the Earth lacks is its own replication.

19:47 You are a bunch of things, not a soul
Mark finds Dennett's 1994 reply collection Get Real, which uses snakes as an example: a snake has no central representation of "mouse," it just responds to prey through three separate sensory systems. Dennett's point is that the perceptual system we take to be a single whole is really a pile of little homunculi each making its own discriminations; you are not an Aristotelian form, a soul, an organisation that runs you — we are all a bunch of things. Christopher objects: failure to integrate information processing doesn't mean there's no self — the two hemispheres of a split-brain patient are also separate, and we don't conclude from that that he has no self; a snake may still have a more ancient, minimal sense of boundary and evaluative experience.

27:39 Reducing experience to discrimination looks a lot like behaviourism
Christopher says he agrees with Dennett 99%, and is stuck on the 1%: when Dennett wants to reduce a person to dispositional states, saying that experiencing red is nothing over and above being able to discriminate red from non-red and being in that discriminative state, it sounds like behaviourism. Seth offers a defence: even if the substrate is just discriminative states, subjective experience, the self, is a composite stitched together out of memory, imagination, representation and symbolic language — it weaves scattered discriminative states into a story with descriptions, meanings and colour, and that story is me. Christopher agrees about the narrative self, but points out that a bat has no metacognitive capacity to construct such a self.

38:54 You can club iguanas, but not rabbits
Mark says "everyone is a world" is a good moral fiction, but he doesn't know how to apply it to animals: Florida has too many iguanas, and he encourages people to go out and club them, which he says is completely fine and humane; swap in a rabbit and he won't accept it. Seth offers an evolutionary explanation: our feelings about animals domesticated over tens of thousands of years, wild animals and reptiles were never the same to begin with, and this doesn't conflict with the self being a narrative centre of gravity. Christopher anchors it in valence: animals are not reflex machines, they are situated perspectives that evaluate, and that is the reason they enter moral consideration — he says that after reading Lars Chittka's The Mind of a Bee, the way he deals with bees changed.

46:10 Take away caring and nothing is left of pain
Mark turns to where Dennett talks specifically about pain: what is the functional relation of pain? If you take away "caring about it, wanting to get away from it," take away everything else, and leave only the sensation of pain, then nothing is left — your not liking pain is itself part of the pain. Mark says this is exactly Dennett's attitude to philosophical zombies: imagine someone whose biology, reactions and even internal relations are exactly like yours, but the light of consciousness never came on — Dennett thinks this is so absurd that it's hard even to explain to scientists.

item.title: Beijing's Central Axis Is Not a Relic — It's a City Operating System Still Running
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.description: The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier in the Kaogong Ji, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.
item.content:encoded:
The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier in the Kaogong Ji, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.

Medium information density, but its strength is restoring the central axis from tourist attraction to a planning logic still in force — suited to anyone interested in cities and organisational design.

7:13 A manual from two thousand years ago is still in use
When the Ming set out to rebuild the capital, they dug up a technical manual more than two thousand years old, the Kaogong Ji (“考工记”). It specified a city four to five kilometres on each side, three gates per side, the palace at the centre, an ancestral temple on one side, the court in front, the market behind, and a Temple of Heaven in the southern suburbs. The historian Jeremiah Jenik says the logic behind this layout was cosmic order: there is a fixed point in the sky, the North Star, so there should be a corresponding fixed point on earth, and the most fitting fixed point is the emperor himself — placing yourself in the palace at the exact centre of the city is placing yourself inside a cosmic order that revolves around you.

9:16 They actually built it to the drawing
The most astonishing thing is not that the Ming dared to use a blueprint over a thousand years old, but how closely they built to it. Overlay the Kaogong Ji drawing on the model at the Beijing Planning Exhibition Hall and the two almost coincide. So Beijing today is still a twenty-first-century city running around a fifteenth-century heart, and that heart follows principles laid down nearly two thousand years ago. Compare London, which grew organically along the Thames: Beijing had the blueprint first, the city second.

11:20 The central axis is a spine, and the city grew out of it
From north to south, the axis strings together the Bird's Nest, the Drum and Bell Towers, Jingshan, the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, and finally Yongdingmen at the southern end. The episode likens it to a spine: everything is planned and expanded outward from this line. Running true north-south and aligned with the heavens, the line has been Beijing's most distinctive feature for six hundred years, and it determines the shape of the city today.

12:22 The right to tell time is the right to rule
The Drum and Bell Towers were the city's timekeeping centre, and the bells were said to carry twenty kilometres. From 1272 all the way to 1924 — the year the last Qing emperor left the Forbidden City — the time struck here was Beijing's official time. The drum was beaten a hundred and eight times every two hours; it was the first sound Beijingers heard in the morning and the last they heard at night. The episode says it is almost as if the emperor were not merely marking time but claiming ownership of time itself.

15:32 Jingshan was piled up from the rubble of the previous dynasty
Jingshan is not a natural hill; it was built artificially by the Yongle Emperor according to feng shui principles. An ideal palace faces south, with water to the south that curves and flows to bring qi and life, and a mountain to the north to block the evil qi coming from that direction and display power. Beijing is too far from the Yan Mountains to the north, so the Ming used rubble from the old Mongol palaces and earth dug out of new water channels to build a symbolic mountain inside the city.

18:52 The Forbidden City was a super-project of nationwide mobilisation
Ten thousand logs were shipped from 1,800 kilometres to the southwest, Suzhou's golden bricks came from 1,100 kilometres to the south — 18 million bricks fired in all — and gold leaf came from Nanjing. A million labourers plus more than a hundred thousand craftsmen built it in fifteen years. From the 1420s to the early twentieth century, twenty-four emperors lived here. Today it receives more than fifteen million visitors a year, making it the most visited historic site on earth.

22:55 A nail-free timber structure can survive a magnitude 9.5 earthquake
These buildings are almost entirely wood, and what lets them stand for centuries is the dogong (斗拱): the dou are the bearing blocks, the gong slot in, and they interlock very tightly. Wood shrinks and warps, and this system lets it deform flexibly while keeping the overall structure intact; in an earthquake every small piece of wood can slide a little, without shearing the bearing blocks or popping screws. Scientists have calculated that this construction could withstand a magnitude 9.5 earthquake, the strongest ever recorded.

23:57 It was struck by lightning within a year of completion
The Forbidden City was not fireproof. Less than a year after it was completed in 1421, the three great halls burned to ashes after a lightning strike. Afterwards 308 bronze vats were installed to store water against the next fire. The detail makes the point: no matter how precise the planning, it cannot stop a single point of failure — you can only add redundancy after the fact.

item.title: Germany's CDU Falls Out of a State Parliament: The Era of the Centre Is Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.description: The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.
item.content:encoded:
The CDU won under 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.

This is a piece of German domestic political commentary, not an interview. Information density is moderate, but it lays out the judgment that "populism has become the mainstream" very clearly. Suited to anyone watching the direction of European politics.

0:00 The CDU is shut out of a state parliament for the first time
In the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, the CDU won under 5% of the vote and therefore holds no seats in that state parliament — the first time this has happened in the history of the Federal Republic. In the same election the AfD took around 38% of the vote, once again becoming the state's largest party. The author calls this the "final nail in the coffin" for Merz: he may hang on as chancellor for a few more weeks or months, but his authority is gone, his capacity to shape the country thoroughly exhausted — in political language, "a dead man walking."

0:00 The CDU's decline came later than the SPD's but is just as fatal
The CDU is the most important party in postwar German history, governing the Federal Republic for 53 of the past 77 years, from Adenauer and Kohl to Merkel, leaving its mark on every aspect of the country. The author notes that in the early 2000s everyone was talking about "the crisis of social democracy," with the SPD falling from over 40% support to record lows; in hindsight, the fate of the centre-left big party was merely a leading indicator of a broader crisis of the entire political centre, and the CDU subsequently walked the same road. The era of what Germans call the Volksparteien — catch-all parties capable of mobilising most of the vote — is effectively over.

0:00 Populists are not a fringe phenomenon but the most important political force
The author says this is the most-asked question of the past decade: "Will the populist wave last, or is it about to peak?" In the summer of 2016, when Trump became the Republican nominee and Britain voted for Brexit, the answer seemed obvious to him; now the answer is undeniable — the populists are here to stay. What looked abnormal a few years ago has, like it or not, become the mainstream. Populist politicians now hold power in the United States, India, Turkey and much of the democratic world, and have a very high probability of taking office in France and Brazil in the coming months. Even where they remain in opposition, they are already strong enough to destroy any sense of business as usual.

0:00 The rise of one extremist party is feeding another
In the Berlin state election, Die Linke took 26% of the vote and emerged the big winner. The party descends from the SED, which ruled East Germany with an iron fist; after reunification it initially appealed mainly to older voters nostalgic for the security of the communist system, and in recent years it has remade itself in the image of the global illiberal left — the author considers it roughly comparable to Zack Polanski's Greens in Britain or the more extreme parts of the DSA in the United States. During the campaign, some of its supporters were filmed chanting "Yalla, Yalla Intifada!"; on election night, the head of a notorious crime family visited the party's election party and cheerfully told the media he felt an affinity with it. The party's leader will very likely become the next mayor of Berlin, which would be the first time an heir to the SED has taken power in the capital.

0:00 Voters under 35 have swung to the two extremes
Another notable feature of the two elections is the age distribution. The SPD and CDU, which once dominated Germany's political landscape, draw most of their support from pensioners. Among voters under 35, Die Linke and the AfD hold unassailable majorities in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From this the author concludes that an even larger tilt toward the extremes will come in the next few years. This also explains why the collapse of the centre is not a one-off election accident: the structure of the electorate itself is pushing the scales toward the two ends.

0:00 Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's left coalition is just an election accident
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, because a batch of other parties all failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering parliament, a broad left coalition just barely won enough votes to govern. But the author stresses that this is an election accident unlikely to repeat — a few thousand votes either way would leave the state completely ungovernable. The point is crucial: when centrist parties fall below the threshold, they don't just lose their own seats, they push the governability of the entire state to the edge of a cliff.

0:00 Don't surrender, and don't deny that the problem is real
The author explicitly rejects two responses. The first is to urge the centre to surrender: if the political middle can't hold, moderates might as well defect to the extremists on "their own side." He thinks this is wrong — neither Die Linke nor the AfD can solve the real problems Germany faces, and despite their enormous differences they have conspicuous similarities, from their ambiguity toward Moscow to their persistent inability to purge antisemites from their own ranks. The second is to keep denying reality: for a decade the centre has attributed the extremists' success to foreign interference, social media algorithms, one candidate's tactical blunder, or the stupidity, sexism or racism of voters. The author says these ways of blinding oneself to the facts in front of you may be comforting, but they are equally dangerous.

item.title: Going overseas: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and the US — go there first so you can get big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.description: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and the US once they're big, but it's exactly backwards — you go there in order to get big. Pick the wrong region and nothing that follows — product 3.0, the channel pyramid — can be built.
item.content:encoded:
Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and the US once they're big, but it's exactly backwards — you go there in order to get big. Pick the wrong region and nothing that follows — product 3.0, the channel pyramid — can be built.

Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas-investing experience into four choices, each counterintuitive but backed by cases and numbers; the back half, on AI rebuilding organisations and pricing, is the densest.

1:30 The old cross-border mega-seller playbook is dead
Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ model popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset — dozens or hundreds of accounts at a time; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. A decade ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and plenty of investors loved them. But a distribution-style company is essentially a traffic-style company: the more stores, the more likely you are to get traffic. When a platform's goods aren't plentiful enough, he doesn't object to distribution; once goods are plentiful enough, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, there are three red lines: goods not matching the listing harms consumers, brushing orders harms other merchants, and slipping in little cards to build private-domain traffic harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel puts enormous weight on consumer experience, and these behaviours run straight into that wall.

4:38 Of the four choices, region comes first
Wei Zhe says it isn't just cross-border e-commerce — all of life is about choice mattering more than effort. He lays out four choices: region, channel, product category, brand positioning. On region he has always argued for seizing the European and American market first, because purchasing power is strong, internet penetration is high, and more importantly a brand can build momentum there. This isn't their invention — when Japanese and Korean brands went global back then, they all seized Europe and America. On category they change their advice every three years: the first three years they backed products common to China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification — Anker's power banks, for instance, were almost identical back then apart from voltage; the second three years they advised overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had all gone overseas and China-abroad commonality offered no differentiation; the most recent three years it's product 3.0 — electrified, chipped, algorithmic.

12:29 You don't go to Europe and the US after getting big — you go there to get big
Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and the US once I'm big’, and he says it's exactly backwards: you go to Europe and the US in order to get big. He cites the swimwear company Cupshe — a husband and wife, 50,000 dollars of inventory, and the first stop was the US. Fifty thousand dollars is sales inventory, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. Looking recently at AI smart hardware, they start from a thousand or ten thousand products on the Kickstarter crowdfunding platform, even taking prepayment before placing orders, with no capital — that too is a great way to test the water. He even advises big companies entering the European and American market to learn from small startups. They always say the needle has to be fine enough to pierce through, and big or small, companies should first nail the four singles: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

20:36 After AI, good companies don't just find demand — they create it
Wei Zhe says that with AI, excellent companies shouldn't go looking for demand; they should lead demand and create demand. He cites a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: it used to be unpowered, and they electrified it, adding a chip and an algorithm — the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, since the movements of the sky follow rules. He wasn't an astronomy hobbyist before but he'd buy one: at home in Silicon Valley you tap once, it automatically aligns Orion for you, tells you three in the morning is the best time, you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it has shot it for you. That lets anyone become a very good astronomy hobbyist. Another example: a cross-border class student doing curtains, which didn't sell well in the US once electrified because American electricians are expensive, so he put a solar panel on the window and turned electric curtains that needed an electrician into something you can DIY; the business went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

24:48 In the AI era, still charging subscriptions means you're behind
Wei Zhe says that in the AI era, still thinking in terms of subscription fees means you're behind again; they're all urging companies toward back-end charging, software charging — what they call tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest approach, a bit like advertising that used to charge by time rather than by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks of vacation this month, isn't a monthly subscription wasting two weeks? They advise that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not go back to the old SaaS model of 9.99 dollars a month. One AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and charges nothing if you don't read; the same for smart bike trainers — you top up, then one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

27:28 Adding AI beats AI-plus
Wei Zhe has a formulation: AI-plus or plus-AI. He flips the phrase around — what he favours more is plus-AI, not today's AI-plus. The difference: plus-AI takes hardware humans have already accepted and makes it AI; AI-plus creates hardware never seen before because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept entirely new hardware. Oura makes a ring, for instance, because you already accepted rings; something that hangs a camera under your neck is harder for me — I've never accepted that hardware. So they're very bullish on adding AI to already-accepted hardware. One capacitive stylus they invested in is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad; it doesn't add another pen, it just makes your pen AI. He also particularly wants to transform one of the top one or two overseas fitness-equipment companies, replacing the fitness instructor on the screen with an AI-generated one — you want a man, it's a man; you want a Black instructor, it's a Black instructor; install two cameras and it can coach your workout with AI.

29:43 Channels aren't flat — they're a pyramid
Wei Zhe says channels aren't about more channels meaning more roads, with each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and rules about which channel a new product launches in first. What counts as a light-goods channel, what counts as the main waist channel for volume — the pyramid design differs by category and by brand. He cites Anker: making power-bank mecha gear seems a bit low, so to enter the consumer-electronics high ground with Soundcore headphones you have to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it actually sells a lot doesn't matter, but it can transform the brand — Apple is the tip of the pyramid. Pop Mart has to open on London's Oxford Street; even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose, but it has to hold that position. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel — when Amazon delists you, you dump it there; you can't sell on Amazon and there too, consumers get confused.

36:14 R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0
Wei Zhe says he really dislikes throwing money at marketing. Many Chinese brands going overseas, or cross-border e-commerce companies, are happy to add 2% of revenue as marketing spend, but consumers don't get it. He asks: do you dare add 2% of revenue as R&D spend? He has met many bosses at the one or two billion scale; at one billion they say 20 million for R&D, and I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem — you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing spend makes the platform happy and consumers get nothing; but 2% thrown into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed a good product speaks for itself, and marketing is just — your R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0; if your thing is good you can amplify it, but if you don't have that 1, never put on a lot of 0s. He gives three signals to judge by: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and crush it with double the performance; second, you sell at the same price as it; third, you sell online and it pushes offline channels to come find you.

item.title: The AI office hype hasn't cleared, and the personal Agent war has already begun | Breaking down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.description: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't even officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't even officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.

Four frontline product people break down the four paths of Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse, and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.

0:00 100,000 users prop up a $10 billion valuation
Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation went from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month the new round being quoted in the market has already reached $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan (潘乱) put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the founder nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can pay the price of the next-generation personal operating system to grab a ticket.

15:16 The line between tool and person is initiative
The biggest difference between this wave of Agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context explained again every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, initiative — setting up automated tasks in Manus still depends on prompts, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't initiative. True initiative is subjective agency — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and proactively comes over to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

18:09 Office Agents organise by project, personal Agents organise by person
The most core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centred on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can drive together. In personal scenarios people care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks; office Agents are the ones that care a lot about task completion rate.

30:28 Town first trades email for the user's right to delegate
The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile app, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC; it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you tap confirm. It goes deeper in the email scenario than any other agent, and overseas it has already achieved fairly viral spread, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and acquire the user's ultimate right to delegate bit by bit.

39:33 Poke didn't break out, and it wasn't a technical limit
Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make a standalone app, but Poke didn't break out. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could have done it completely at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-delegation route, able to connect to credit cards, screen and microphone, booking flights and buying things for you — things users had never seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive-push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't take the step of "finishing the thing for you".

42:39 A cloud Agent has to handle three environments
Mark says doing a cloud agent was a painful lesson: a local agent and a cloud agent are completely two different things. To do personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere — you can't be unreachable just because the computer screen is off. On the cloud you have to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context passing between the three are very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably on the cloud took at least two months; setting aside detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

50:39 Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two businesses
Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios; the relationship is more like you paying to hire a personal assistant, which naturally filters for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, a shopping guide, a broker: although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, and the scenarios they cut into and the users they filter out are different too.

1:14:07 Favourites folders may be noise to an Agent
The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was about extracting what you like to eat from ingredients saved on Instagram, generating a shopping list, adjusting the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then completing the shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision-and-transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users complete transactions is absolutely not among the top scenarios users want to solve; users more want to solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in favourites folders; the truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram favourites may themselves be noise to an agent.

item.content:encoded:
On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as certain — from forcing her daughter to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as gospel — each one first learned in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.

For parents who want to interrogate their own parenting methodology. Medium information density, heavy on personal narrative, but the ten reflections are clearly structured, and the back half — on the ‘village’ and on the couple relationship — is more valuable than the front half.

6:00 Forcing the medicine won the behavior and lost the relationship
The host recalls her three-year-old daughter refusing antibiotics; she held her down and forced the medicine in, and her daughter threw most of it back up. That night her husband Alvin stayed with their daughter in the bathroom for an hour, calmly saying the whole time, ‘I'm willing to do anything, but we're not leaving until we figure this out,’ and in the end the daughter finished the whole course herself — small sips of medicine with small sips of water, then a small piece of chocolate to take the taste away. The host says the difference wasn't that her husband was more patient, but that he wasn't solving a behavior — he was understanding what would actually help the child do this thing. What the child needed was autonomy over the process, and to feel that she and her parents were on the same team, rather than being held down to do something.

9:19 The authoritative parenting framework rests on 146 white children
The host says she uncritically accepted the conclusion that ‘authoritative is the best parenting style’ early on, because every blog and every study said so. It wasn't until she made the episode on corporal punishment that she found a paper co-authored by Diana Baumrind defending parents' ability to spank their children, and started digging. She found that this framework — cited more than 26,000 times and defining sixty years of parenting research — was originally based on just 146 white, middle-class preschoolers in the town where Baumrind lived. She calls this evidence of her own insufficient critical thinking, and says she now asks at the macro level ‘does this theory make sense,’ and at the micro level ‘does it fit this specific child in front of me.’

17:41 Not punishing your kid doesn't mean being ruled by your kid
The host says she once believed that without punishment and consequences children would run wild — she even stood in the shower when her daughter was four months old thinking ‘how do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom.’ Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had treated ‘obedience’ as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing was a battle. Once, recording for the host to see, she deliberately used no threats, no punishments and no rewards, and simply asked her two-year-old son ‘why don't you want to brush your teeth.’ He couldn't put it into words — he just called out ‘Mama’ and buried his head in her chest. She realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and they sang a song together, and he brushed his own teeth — the whole thing took under five minutes.

21:31 ‘I need you to take out the trash’ is not a need
The host says that looking back, she didn't understand what a ‘need’ was — she thought saying ‘I need you to take out the trash’ to her husband was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born the two of them almost never argued: mountain biking in summer, skiing in winter, because the ad agency they worked for represented resorts and paid them in vouchers. After their daughter was born everything changed: during his three weeks of paternity leave her husband would fetch her anything she wanted, and the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for ‘collaboration, partnership, having her effort seen’ that actually pried open the problems between them; before that she carried a large amount of resentment inside her with no idea how to handle it.

24:01 When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person who interrupted you
The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted — the moment her husband interrupts her she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage a package needed. She always assumed the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he stopped interrupting, everything would be fine. Recording in July 2018 with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it on the spot to her father, a special education teacher who would treat sixteen-year-olds like ten-year-olds and who, for a stretch, lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, and her daughter said ‘Don't interrupt me, Mama,’ and her husband looked at her and said ‘She is you.’ She says that was the moment she realized it had never just been about the two people in the room, and out of it she developed the ‘Tame Your Triggers’ course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

30:27 The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations for her child
The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, the word ‘me’ cut out of the board on one cover and ‘you’ embossed on the other when you flipped it over — the concept being ‘you came out of me.’ On the ‘me’ side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the ‘you’ side she wrote to Carys, whom she had not yet met. She reads out the earliest batch of ‘expectations for you’: I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of child who shakes hands with people instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like both roughhousing and pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope that when you fall you pick yourself up and say ‘I'm okay.’ She says looking back now, her biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person, to let them be their whole self and witness it, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

33:14 Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
The host says she once thought she would play the role of ‘enforcer’ — she even wrote ‘I hope you can love me as much as he does’ on her pregnancy expectations list. She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what actually planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: principle two is to reconsider your demands — ‘maybe when a child won't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child, it's what you're asking’; principle five is to change the way you look, not just the way you act — when you see your child doing the thing you asked them not to do, your first reaction is curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; principle ten is ‘attribute to your child the best motive consistent with the observed facts,’ and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to ‘consistent with the observed behavior,’ because ‘there are no facts, only what we observe.’

39:07 The couple relationship isn't a different subject — it's the same one
The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things; when she started the parenting membership eight years ago she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module, because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her parenting shift toward collaboration was relatively easy, because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but with Alvin she had been together ten years and had never learned how to disagree, because most of that time was spent doing hobbies they loved, and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she took Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same thing she had been doing with her child all these years — while also believing the Gottman method itself has a few key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments, using modified tools, and one couple — where the husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue — became willing to talk after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him, and they reached an agreement to move forward in that same session.

item.title: NPR's comment section was flagged as bots. It was actually a group of middle schoolers.
