Light Street's Glen Kacher sees AI as a 15-to-20-year rebuild of the computing stack, and only a third of the first leg is done; the real risk is not over-investment in CapEx but power and local politics slowing construction.

An investor running a tech hedge fund in the heart of Silicon Valley strings AI compute, semiconductors, open-source models and the power bottleneck into one investable chain of judgment, at high information density.

7:16 Buy only the best company, never the second or third
Over 13 years at Integral Capital, Kacher made 46 private investments, and the lesson he drew is: do not buy the second- or third-best company in an industry, always buy the best one you can get. The reason is that in tech the leader takes two-thirds of the market, the number two gets 20% to 25% at most, and everyone else fights over scraps. Higher margins plus a dominant share compound the lead. But he also concedes that incumbents in tech get disrupted, and disruption usually comes not from big companies but from small ones — AI and the semiconductors behind AI are exactly the test case for that rule.

8:17 Nvidia's moat is underappreciated
Kacher says many people assume Nvidia will lose its roughly 85% share of the AI accelerator market, and the shift to inference does give competitors an opening. But he thinks the market currently underestimates Nvidia's own capacity to innovate. He describes the evolution of inference chips as an alphabet progression from CPU to FPU to GPU to XPU, where X stands for the unknown: Google has TPU, there are other approaches such as Trainium, and Nvidia itself bought the Grok inference line. He judges that inference will ultimately be a bigger market than training, so there will be many chip forms and many opportunities to innovate.

21:51 Four semiconductor companies are 40% of the portfolio
TSMC, Nvidia, Broadcom and AMD make up roughly 40% of Light Street's public holdings, a highly concentrated portfolio. Kacher's logic: concentrate capital where innovation is densest, and right now the densest place is the core of AI accelerated computing. Nvidia has more than 80% of the GPU networking market and AMD is catching up; as agentic AI becomes the next growth driver, AMD has a unique edge because it is one of the two big players in both desktop and server CPUs; Broadcom has built TPUs for Google for years and now has opportunities with big players such as OpenAI; TSMC fabs for all three, so it wins no matter who wins, an almost oligopolistic or even monopolistic position.

26:01 Open-source models are fighting a price war
Kacher thinks the battle between Anthropic and OpenAI is happening in real time, and that Google remains a player thanks to Gemini and its search distribution advantage, so it cannot be ruled out. But the battlefield really emerging is open-source models: they are free, can be downloaded to run on local hardware, or run on someone else's commoditized hardware in the cloud, competing directly with the two big companies' expensive frontier models. He judges that early signals show both approaches have their place. He also points to the regulatory problem: open-source models can be put into your own software and adjusted to your needs, and regulators actually have few options, because these models are already out in the wild.

33:14 Someone was already saying GPUs would do AI in 2005
Kacher recalls that at Integral, Kleiner Perkins partner Bill Joy mentioned a group of engineers at Caltech using GPUs for early AI computation, around 2005 or 2006, and Bill Joy's conclusion was that GPUs would be the chip architecture best suited to AI computation. It stayed in his head. Later, on every visit to Nvidia, Jensen would talk about AI, but at the time AI was only a tiny end market for Nvidia, and crypto mattered far more. In the second half of 2022 the crypto crash and AI's takeoff happened at the same time, the market was more focused on crypto and pushed the stock down, which gave them the chance to build a position in Nvidia.

45:36 The giants are not over-investing, they are catching up
Faced with the challenge that AI could be over-provisioned like fiber, Kacher's answer is: Amazon, Microsoft and Google are building the compute stack in partnership with Anthropic and OpenAI, and the question is how far ahead of demand they plan. His judgment is that today they are not ahead, they are behind and catching up. Bears expect them to over-invest, but that has not happened today. He concedes there are real bottlenecks, including the memory companies and TSMC, which cannot invest as fast as they would like, so today demand still runs far ahead of supply, and the pessimism around AI is misplaced.

52:47 A fifteen-year cycle, and only a third of it is done
Kacher likens AI to the shift from client-server to internet architecture, a computing cycle that happens roughly every 15 to 25 years. The old technology was a search-then-retrieve model, with data sitting in databases; AI generates a custom answer for your question and your data on every use, and is far more compute-intensive. His pacing: infrastructure development takes roughly 5 to 10 years, years 6 to 16 are when the platform or operating system takes shape, and years 11 to 21 are when applications become the main venue for enterprise investment and innovation. By that framework, roughly a third of the first leg is done, and the whole cycle is at least 15 to 20 years.

53:48 Power and local politics have become the new bottleneck
Kacher treats political resistance to data centers as a real risk: any bottleneck that slows technology adoption is a problem. He says it is not yet a big problem today, but it is an emerging one. His solution is that the industry has to explain itself proactively: Northern Virginia, as the data center capital of the world, has brought the area tax revenue and blue-collar demand for electricians, plumbers and construction workers, a shot in the arm for the economy. He mentions a data center project in San Mateo that plans to put Bloom Energy natural gas fuel cells behind the meter, with almost no emissions and almost no noise, and residents still opposed it because they had "heard data centers are bad." He sees this as an education problem, requiring project-by-project explanation of energy, jobs and tax revenue, from local to national.

item.title: The Pizza Tracker: We Were Trained to Pay for Fake Progress Bars
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-planetmoney-披萨追踪器-我们被驯化成愿意为假进度条买单/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-planetmoney-披萨追踪器-我们被驯化成愿意为假进度条买单/
item.description: Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool and became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.
item.content:encoded:
Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool and became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.

Medium information density, but the second half on "deliberate slowdowns" and "fake progress bars" is worth the price. Suited to listeners interested in product design and consumer psychology.

2:07 The 30-minute guarantee sold control, not speed
Domino's once promised delivery in 30 minutes or it was free. The guarantee made drivers speed, led to deaths and lawsuits, and was eventually dropped. But David Halbenstricker has a theory: the guarantee was popular not just because it was fast, but because it gave customers a sense of control. In the early 2000s Domino's commissioned a study and found that the customer's psychology after ordering a pizza is a roller coaster: the peak is at the moment of ordering, then it slides all the way down — "Where's my pizza? Did they lose my order?" However long the actual wait, what customers hate is the waiting itself.

8:16 The internal tool had to work first, before the customer side
Executives didn't initially want to build a pizza tracker, because tracking every pizza at every store was too time-consuming and looked like a gimmick. What they were really obsessed with was "out-the-door time." A UK franchisee put the out-the-door times of five to ten nearby stores on a single display so they competed against each other, and paid cash bonuses to the top-ranked stores. After David's boss visited the UK, he had David replicate the system in the US. David connected each store's out-the-door time to a central system and built a real-time dashboard. The CEO called it the thing that drove performance most in his tenure.

11:25 The tracker was a byproduct of the internal system
David and a colleague realized they already had a system tracking every pizza, so they decided to "hitch a ride" and build a customer-facing tracker. In 2006 most people didn't have smartphones; FedEx, UPS and Amazon could track packages, but on a timescale of days, not minutes. Real-time tracking of pizza progress was entirely new. The designer's interface looked like a horizontal thermometer: order, prep, bake, box, delivery — each completed step turned the next segment red. When David saw the mockup he said: "That's a hot dog. We're a pizza company, why is there a hot dog?" But executives liked it, and decided to launch before the Super Bowl.

15:36 Designers use the pizza tracker as a meeting prop
Shuya Gong was a design director at IDEO and later taught design at Harvard. Consulting for many companies in the mid-2010s, she found one of the most effective ways to open a meeting was to order a pizza on the spot, project the tracker onto a big screen, and ask the client: "How do you feel right now?" She says you can feel the anxiety rise or fall in your body, feel the reassurance and groundedness. Then you can ask: which of those parts do you want your users to feel when they use your product? The pizza tracker became shorthand in her design circle: whenever a client involved waiting, she'd say "they need a pizza tracker."

17:39 The tracker manufactures a "labor illusion"
Shuya says one reason the pizza tracker caught on is that as shopping became more digital, the tracker replicated something important from the physical world — watching other people work. Online experiences lack that visibility, so people get impatient more easily. Researchers found that reminding customers there is labor behind a product makes them value it more, and called it the "labor illusion." Shuya also describes a stranger mechanism: the tracker changes our perception of time. Like walking somewhere and finding the return trip feels shorter because the route is familiar and has landmarks. The pizza tracker gives us a familiar route and landmarks — pizza being made, on the road, out for delivery — making the wait feel shorter.

19:47 Banks deliberately slow transfers to fake a wait
Working with banks and fintech companies in the mid-2010s, Shuya found their problem was the opposite of Domino's: customers weren't used to transfers being so fast. Two computers talk, confirm the amount, and the money is gone — no road to cross, no cheese to melt. But to people used to money taking a while to arrive, instant arrival "feels suspicious." So companies deliberately slow down the "money tracker," withholding real-time feedback and adding a buffer that makes you wait. Shuya says this is intentionally slowing time, adding meaningful friction so that in the waiting you feel the seriousness and weight of the transfer. The host presses: isn't that advising lying to customers? Shuya says she prefers to understand it as "curating the experience," adding back the physicality that existed in the traditional experience, to make people comfortable.

21:48 TurboTax and Uber progress bars may be fake
TurboTax pops up animations during filing saying "we're checking your deductions and credits." But a few years ago someone looked at the code and found the animation was identical for everyone, in every situation, and took the same amount of time. The question is: is TurboTax trying to reassure us during the terrifying ordeal of filing taxes, or using the labor illusion to make us feel a big payment is worth it? Uber is similar: the host repeatedly got updated pickup times, but the car almost always arrived later than promised. It felt like the tracker was part of a deliberate deception — to make you choose Uber over Lyft, to keep you from cancelling, to get you standing on the street early. The show reached out to TurboTax and Uber; TurboTax didn't respond, Uber didn't arrange an interview but shared some data suggesting their pickup times are fairly accurate.

25:52 Field test: the pizza tracker is mostly real
Nick biked to a local Domino's to stake it out, while Alex ordered a half-Hawaiian, half-pepperoni pizza at home and monitored the tracker in real time. Nick ordered a pepperoni pizza in the store as cover. The tracker showed "Ivan" making the pizza, but when Nick asked the staff their name, they said "Alex." The tracker also showed a "quality check," but Nick saw no quality inspector. David had explained, though, that because Domino's uses conveyor ovens, the bake time is nearly fixed, so the tracker automatically jumps to the next step after a set time. Eventually the pizza came out, was boxed, and was driven off by Alex (aka Ivan), with Nick chasing on his bike and nearly being taken for a stalker. Alex hit "delivered" at Nick's door and the tracker updated quickly. Conclusion: the tracker is mostly accurate, but "Ivan is making it" and the "quality check" are fake.

item.title: AI Proves in Half an Hour a Math Theorem Humans Couldn't Crack in a Year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.description: A stuck L^p problem, and AI delivers a five-page proof in half an hour, compressing a 60-page paper down to its core lemma and pushing the threshold for continuous density from 588 to 9.
item.content:encoded:
A stuck L^p problem, and AI delivers a five-page proof in half an hour, compressing a 60-page paper down to its core lemma and pushing the threshold for continuous density from 588 to 9.

If you care about what AI can actually do in pure mathematics, this episode gives a concrete, verifiable case: not assisted computation, but a proof structure humans hadn't thought of.

0:18 For the first time, AI had a good idea
The speaker says this is the first time he has encountered a model that "really had a good idea" on a problem he had worked on for a long time, and that the idea led to "very elegant efficient progress." Note his wording: it isn't that AI did the computation for him, it's that AI produced a proof approach he hadn't thought of. He credits the result to Astra, and says it was done only last week.

8:13 The key theorem: absolute continuity automatically carries L^p
The core theorem is: if a self-similar measure μ is absolutely continuous, then its density automatically lies in some L^p with p greater than 1. What actually excites the speaker isn't this fact itself, but that p is quantitative — p can be expressed explicitly in terms of the mass μ gives to small balls. Because p is quantitative, one can bring over the methods used to study explicit absolute continuity, construct explicit L^p examples, and from there get to continuous density.

12:27 p can never be made uniform
The speaker specifically warns: p can never be made uniform. For any dimension d and any p greater than 1, there exists some self-similar measure that lies in L^1 but not in L^p. So this quantitative result cannot be read as "all absolutely continuous self-similar measures have uniform L^p integrability" — it is a case-by-case bound that depends on the mass distribution.

23:45 Splitting λ into odd and even parts
The trick for proving continuous density: split the random series of the Bernoulli convolution into odd and even terms; after factoring a λ out of the odd part, what remains is exactly the even part. So μ_λ equals the convolution of μ_{λ²} with itself. If λ² falls in the range where Solomyak proved L^2 holds almost surely, then the convolution of two L^2 functions is continuous, and μ_λ has continuous density. This is the bridge from an L^2 result to continuity.

34:17 A 60-page paper compressed into 5 pages
The speaker says the core idea was in fact one he and a collaborator already had, but that AI was "extremely elegant and efficient" in using it. Varju's paper is 60 pages, his own paper is also very long, and AI compressed the passage from one result to another into 5 pages; and after "maybe a bit of a weakening," another 5 pages gets a stronger conclusion. He stresses that this is not AI thinking up the core idea for him, it's AI combining known tools in a way he "could have never" done.

36:18 Half an hour to run, 50 hours to formalise
Asked about runtime, the speaker says "not long, maybe half an hour." The whole result was then formalised in Lean, which took about 50 hours. He also mentions tricks like goal command that let the model "really try hard." The comparison: it might have taken him a year, and "if you sent me this paper to referee, I would like who is this person?"

39:21 The threshold for continuous density goes from 588 to 9
For the case λ = 1 - 1/n, AI proves μ_λ is continuous when n is greater than 588 — the speaker says this is not yet the result of him pushing the constant, "if I push the constant, I could easily push the constant more." Even more striking is another result: absolutely continuous when n is greater than 9, which the speaker says "I could not dare think I could prove"; he himself pushed for two and a half hours to get to 9, while the ideal target is 3.

43:23 The key lemma comes from an obscure paper
At the heart of the proof is a lemma from geometric measure theory: for an L^1 positive function f, if the mass of a set inside a small ball is small and the integral of f over that set is also small, then f lies in some explicit L^p, with p given explicitly by C, ε, A. The speaker says this lemma is "not too difficult to prove," about a page, but "extremely difficult to find because it's not a very well-known fact" — it was dug out of some random papers.

item.title: Looney Tunes animator Chuck Jones: A character isn't drawn, it's thought up
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freshair-乐一通-动画师-角色不是画出来的-是想出来的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freshair-乐一通-动画师-角色不是画出来的-是想出来的/
item.description: Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which is how he made Daffy both cowardly and swaggering, and made Bugs Bunny strike back only after being provoked.
item.content:encoded:
Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which is how he made Daffy both cowardly and swaggering, and made Bugs Bunny strike back only after being provoked.

The first half, the Chuck Jones interview, is information-dense; the second half, the Cassandra Wilson segment, is mostly music appreciation, so you can listen to just the interview portion.

0:00 Bugs Bunny's violence wouldn't pass review today
Comedian Dustin Nickerson tried showing classic cartoons to his young daughter and found they hadn't become harmless with time: plenty of characters have speech impediments, and the behavior is highly aggressive. Pepe Le Pew physically holds a female character so she can't leave, while other characters murder each other — the Coyote wants to kill the bird. This runs counter to the cartoon impression in viewers' memories that "everyone is friends."

4:04 A shelved Warner film was saved by an independent distributor
After Coyote vs. Acme was finished, Warner Bros. Discovery shelved it and wrote it off for tax purposes. This year an independent distributor bought the rights for $50 million, and last month it finally opened. The film played in relatively few theaters across the U.S., but it has already recouped almost its entire cost domestically, with another $30 million overseas. The movie itself is about the Coyote suing the Acme Corporation, inspired by Ian Frazier's 1990 parody piece in The New Yorker.

7:07 Daffy is cowardly and swaggering at the same time
Chuck Jones said what makes Daffy funny is that he rushes in and fears to take a step at the same time, is sycophantic and domineering at the same time — like when we go into the boss's office to ask for a raise, swaggering at the door but fawning once inside, except Daffy does both at once. He admitted he couldn't understand "crazy" characters, so he always had to "pasteurize" a character and figure out who he is. He stressed that the point of character animation isn't what the character looks like, nor how it's drawn, but "who he is."

9:11 Bugs Bunny is a comedy hero, not a comedy loser
Jones first did Duck Amuck with Daffy, then later did Rabbit Rampage with Bugs Bunny, and the same setup didn't hold, because Bugs isn't that kind of character. He classified Bugs as a comedy hero, whereas the line of comedians running through Chaplin and Buster Keaton are half-losers, more like ordinary people. He liked Daffy because Daffy keeps going forward, to the point where Jones himself would stop for fear of what others would think.

10:14 A two-hour "yes session" where no negatives are allowed
After 1946, Warner's cartoons were directed by three men: Fritz Freeling, Bob McKimpson and Jones. Whoever had an idea for a film called the other directors and the writers into a meeting they called a "yes session": for two hours no one was allowed to say anything negative, and if you had nothing to contribute you shut up. The result was that everyone participated in everyone else's films, but each director had absolute control over the content of his own, with no infighting among them. Jones also admitted that if a good gag he'd given was used by Freeling and the audience laughed, he naturally wanted to go throw up — that's human nature, and it was the Daffy in him.

13:25 The narrower the rules, the better the comedy
Jones believed that in comedy, the more you narrow and restrict a character, the better it works: once Chaplin put on the Little Tramp outfit, what he could do was locked down. Once Roadrunner and Coyote were fixed in the American Southwest desert, the rules followed — Roadrunner has to stay on the road, can never hurt Coyote, and Coyote can only hurt himself through the unlucky Acme products he buys, with no sound in the whole film except "beep-beep." Bugs Bunny is too powerful and easily becomes a bully, so every film first lets him live his own life in his natural rabbit environment, until someone comes to take his hide or his life, and only then does he strike back.

16:30 Hiding one dirty frame in a twenty-fourth of a second
Jones admitted that Warner's animators all drew that kind of pornographic cartoon privately. He himself would sometimes slip a single frame — a twenty-fourth of a second — of a dirty image into a Pepe Le Pew film, then call the office manager over and say there seemed to be a little glitch here that he couldn't figure out. He knew no one could see it, but the manager would be shocked on the spot. He always kept a replacement frame on hand just in case, but he enjoyed doing it, in his words, to "reduce him to moccasins."

17:31 The networks cut films until they were incomprehensible
Jones said his scenes and lines were never censored; that job was left to the "brilliant people" at the networks, and what they cut made the whole film incomprehensible. Both CBS and ABC did it. What he found absurd was that the Roadrunner series, the one most complained about for violence, actually has no violence — Roadrunner never hurts Coyote, and Coyote is simply the victim of his own incompetence.

item.title: The last IMO problem AI could not solve, and its value is not in the answer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-karpathy-ai-解不出的最后一道-imo-题-价值不在答案/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-karpathy-ai-解不出的最后一道-imo-题-价值不在答案/
item.description: In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants got full marks on Problem 6, and every AI was stuck on it. What makes it hard is not computation — it is that you must first understand, first have taste, and only then put pen to paper. And that is exactly what reinforcement learning struggles most to train.
item.content:encoded:
In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants got full marks on Problem 6, and every AI was stuck on it. What makes it hard is not computation — it is that you must first understand, first have taste, and only then put pen to paper. And that is exactly what reinforcement learning struggles most to train.

The bulk of this episode is a complete walkthrough of one math problem, not AI industry analysis. Only the last 5 minutes discuss the relationship between AI and mathematics, but those 5 minutes are worth hearing.

0:00 What blocks AI is not computation, it is patience
On 2025 IMO Problem 6, of more than 600 top contestants worldwide, fewer than 1% earned full marks. By 2025, models from several institutions could already answer every other problem, and got stuck only on this one. DeepMind research director Thang Luong's explanation: the model has no patience — it will not spend time understanding the problem or developing a feel for it, and instead starts solving immediately. Karpathy adds a second reason: the model has no sense of what makes a problem or a strategy beautiful, and the solution to this problem depends precisely on aesthetic judgment.

6:11 Genius is really the residue of experience
Facing this problem, the most obvious construction is to put all the X's on the diagonal and cover the remaining region with horizontal tiles, giving 2(n-1) pieces. But this construction is too obvious to be the answer IMO wants. Karpathy inserts a seemingly unrelated cube-cutting brainteaser here: a 3x3x3 cube cut into 27 small cubes, where you may rearrange the pieces after each cut — what is the minimum number of cuts? The answer is 6, because each of the 6 faces of the very center small cube requires its own separate cut. This proof idea — fix your attention on one face of the internal structure — is exactly the key to the tiling problem that follows.

12:17 The most efficient tiling has every tile touching four X's
Highlight the four edges of every X, and each time you place a tile, switch off the edges it touches. In an inefficient tiling, a tile touches only 1 or even 0 X's; in an efficient tiling, every tile touches 4 X's. This yields a conjecture: the optimal tiling should make as many tiles as possible touch 4 distinct X's. But look further: an X cannot sit in the middle of a tile's edge — that would make the two tiles above and below conflict on the left, because a single column cannot contain two X's. The X must sit at a corner of the tiles, with four tiles pinwheeling around it. With square tiles of side length k, you can tile a large grid of side length k². And 2025 happens to be 45², a coincidence that makes the construction look extremely promising.

19:27 Highlight only one direction and the proof misses the tiles on one side
Highlight the edges of all X's: 4k² edges in total, each tile touches at most 4, and subtracting the 4 boundary edges that need not be touched gives the lower bound k²-1. But the target lower bound is k²+2k-3, off by a term proportional to k. The problem is that only the right edges are highlighted: the correspondence this yields is tight on the right side of the diagram, but misses a large number of tiles concentrated on the left. Switching to any other single direction is the same — the missed tiles always cluster on one side. Karpathy says mathematics rewards you for respecting symmetry, and punishes you for not respecting it: pick an arbitrary direction, and the weakness shows up in the inequality.

27:38 Cut the grid into four regions, highlight each edge only once
The solution is to draw two paths: one going up-right along the X's, one going down-right, dividing the whole diagram into four regions. If an X is in the right region, highlight its right edge; if in the top region, highlight its top edge — left, right, top, bottom each govern one region. An X lying on a boundary highlights two edges. This both supplies the missing highlighted edges and guarantees that each tile touches at most one highlighted edge — because when a tile sits in the left region, the X above it cannot highlight a bottom edge, the X below it cannot highlight a top edge, and the X to its left cannot highlight a right edge. This diagram is the core of the entire proof.

31:48 The problem reduces to a pure permutation problem
Label each X with the row it sits in; since each row contains exactly one X, these labels form a permutation of 1 to k². The up-right path corresponds to an increasing subsequence, the down-right path to a decreasing subsequence. Let LIS be the length of the longest increasing subsequence and LDS the longest decreasing subsequence; the total number of highlighted edges is then k² + LIS + LDS - 4 (or +1 when the two paths intersect, making it -3). To prove the target lower bound k²+2k-3, it suffices to prove LIS + LDS ≥ 2k, that is, that the average of the two is at least k. At this point the grid has vanished entirely, and what remains is a pure fact about permutations.

39:59 The proof of Erdős-Szekeres is itself a gem
This pure permutation fact is the Erdős-Szekeres theorem: in any permutation, the product of the lengths of the longest increasing subsequence and the longest decreasing subsequence is at least the length n of the permutation. An IMO contestant could simply cite the theorem and finish, but Karpathy chooses to give the proof too. The method is to label each position with a pair of numbers: the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending there, and the length of the longest decreasing subsequence ending there. Because the numbers in a permutation are all distinct, these two label pairs must differ for any two positions — if the later number is larger, the first label increases by at least one; if smaller, the second label increases by at least one. Plot these label pairs as coordinate points: the longest increasing subsequence is the width of the bounding box, the longest decreasing subsequence is the height, and width times height equals the number of lattice points, which is the length of the permutation.

48:08 Beyond the proof there is another layer: making the proof feel obvious
Karpathy says knowing a proof is only a very small part of deeply understanding mathematics. When he and Nishad Dulkhar made this video, their first reaction on seeing the original proof was, "I know it's true, but how would anyone come up with this?" What they wanted to contribute was not a new proof but a narrative, so that when viewers arrive at the proof it no longer feels like it appeared out of nowhere. He has a name for this: motivated explanation. This bears directly on AI and mathematics: if a machine can generate proofs but does not bring human understanding, then it has completely lost its meaning. And academia has long used "proof" as a proxy metric for progress, which exposes an urgent need — for a new, independent way to measure whether a publication actually advances human understanding.

item.title: NASA Administrator: We're Not a Procurement Agency, We're a Nuclear-Powered NASA
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-nasa-局长-我们不是采购机构-是核动力-nasa/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-nasa-局长-我们不是采购机构-是核动力-nasa/
item.description: Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and to hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.
item.content:encoded:
Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and to hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.

This is the policy manifesto of NASA's new administrator, with information density concentrated on the lunar south pole, nuclear power and the Mars plan — though the back half of the interview is soft, with mediocre Q&A.

2:06 NASA used to spread resources around to please everyone
Isaacman divides NASA's problems into two kinds: externally imposed and self-inflicted. Partnering for partnership's sake turned partnerships into a drag on missions rather than an accelerator. The result is that Orion cannot inject into low lunar orbit the way Apollo did; the previous administration cancelled Mars Sample Return because the cost would exceed an aircraft carrier. He also says NASA built programs that are "too big to fail and too expensive to ever really succeed," betting they would survive across administrations. Core capabilities were rented out, outsourced or simply lost, and progress that should have taken months turned into years at greatly increased cost.

3:07 The lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V from sixty years ago
He offers a jarring comparison: China's rockets were designed when locomotives still burned coal, and today China operates 25,000 miles of high-speed rail and is only a few years from its own Apollo 11 moment. Meanwhile NASA's lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V at converting launch mass into payload headed to the Moon; the gap between Artemis 1 and Artemis 2 is longer than all 12 Gemini missions of sixty years ago combined. The lunar space station puts astronauts in a position to look down on the most coveted lunar real estate, rather than working on the surface and occupying it.

7:07 The lunar south pole has only a few good parking spots
The Moon's surface area is roughly that of Africa, but the south pole is only about the size of Washington, D.C., and the usable permanently shadowed craters are limited. Those craters hold water ice, and the environment is harsher than Mars itself; the crater walls can also provide near-permanent solar illumination. So good landing sites are very few. He notes that a Starship-sized vehicle landing on the lunar surface would blast out a crater and throw debris, further shrinking the usable spots. China's robotic mission is targeting Shackleton Crater next year, and China and Russia are also cooperating on a nuclear-powered lunar base.

8:07 Launching a 100-kilowatt fission reactor in 2028
NASA is saying goodbye to failed nuclear programs that have not left the lab since 1965, and in 2028 will launch SR1 Freedom, a 100-kilowatt fission reactor. The mission will fly past Mars and release Skyfall, carrying three Ingenuity-class helicopters to scout underground ice and future landing sites with ground-penetrating radar. He calls this the beginning of a "nuclear-powered NASA," turning its workforce and facilities back to missions that are nearly impossible and have no obvious commercial case. SR2, SR3 and SR4 follow, with targets including Enceladus, Europa and Titan — moons with oceans and complex chemistry.

23:22 The hardest part of Mars is not getting there, it's coming back
Pure chemical propulsion can also send astronauts to Mars, at a speed comparable to going to the Moon, and the habitation problem was solved long ago. The hard part is how to come back: you need to manufacture propellant on the Martian surface, and the plan is robots plus football-field-sized solar arrays, with the dust from dust storms regularly blown off. He says doing this under one Earth atmosphere and 1G is already extremely difficult. NASA's answer is to stop doing what industry already does well and turn to next-generation capabilities with no commercial case: fission power, plus a chemically boosted nuclear transfer vehicle using krypton or xenon rather than manufacturing propellant on the Martian surface.

25:23 Hiring isn't hard, retaining talent is
NASA's internship program accepts only 1% of applicants, so there is no recruiting problem early on. The question is whether it can keep people. If NASA does the same work as SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke and ULA while still using fifty-year-old space shuttle hardware, it will lose talent. His approach: once a breakthrough has a commercial case, such as launch, NASA becomes one customer among many, hands the capability to industry and moves on to the next new thing. SR1 is only the beginning of a nuclear-powered NASA — their Nautilus — and a whole nuclear fleet will follow.

27:24 Nuclear propulsion is essentially an ion thruster in space
He explains the principle: the ion thrusters on Starlink satellites use solar power to ionize and accelerate krypton or xenon and expel it, with extremely high exhaust velocity, very low thrust but very high efficiency, so propellant lasts a long time. The farther from the Sun, the more useless solar power becomes, and near Jupiter it is essentially negligible. At that point you switch to the heat of a nuclear reactor, starting at 100 kilowatts and possibly scaling to 250 kilowatts or even megawatts. The reactor should run as hot as possible, using high-temperature materials and a closed Brayton cycle to convert heat to electricity, then drive the same thrusters, just scaled up from 12, 14, 25 kilowatts.

28:24 NASA doesn't lack budget, it lacks capital allocation ability
He says NASA does not have a top line problem, but has long been bad at capital allocation, partly by NASA's own choice and partly imposed by others. The budget is now $25 billion. He asks how many founders are in the room, and says $25 billion is a lot of money that can build pretty amazing hardware. In aeronautics, he complains that NASA's aeronautics budget is used to subsidize high-TRL programs at big contractors — for example, a forty-year-old engine that wants another 3% fuel efficiency and gets NASA to pay for it. He wants to return to radical airframe and engine designs.

item.title: Wanting to Save the World Is No Excuse for a Monopoly Agreement
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-moneystuff-想拯救世界-不是搞垄断协议的借口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-moneystuff-想拯救世界-不是搞垄断协议的借口/
item.description: AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is, legally, a textbook antitrust conspiracy — wanting to save the world is not a defense.
item.content:encoded:
AI labs want to jointly slow down model development, but four giants sitting down to talk about deceleration is, legally, a textbook antitrust conspiracy — wanting to save the world is not a defense.

Three segments: the insider-trading evidence problem, Dario's deceleration memo, and pension privatization. Medium information density; the last two segments are worth more.

2:05 Suing a hundred John Does doesn't fly with the judge
Susquehanna spotted heavy buying of short-dated puts in Chinese brokerage stocks before cross-border trading was restricted, so it sued 100 John Does and tried to freeze the accounts. But the judge denied the preliminary injunction: it could not be shown that all 100 were conspiring to trade on inside information. Levine's breakdown is that maybe only a tiny few actually got the inside information, and the rest just saw the tape move and piled in — and piling into a publicly visible move is itself entirely legal. The ones who can actually figure out who is who are the securities regulators, not the market makers who got picked off.

8:13 The market maker's loss may not be that big
Susquehanna claims it lost about $70 million on those puts, but Levine points out that this is only half the story: as an options market maker, after selling puts it would normally hedge immediately, maybe by shorting the stock, maybe by buying puts back from another client or another market maker. If Citadel Securities and Susquehanna were both selling and both buying that day, they were effectively betting against each other and should in theory be suing each other. So the "lost $70 million" number obscures the fact that they were also hedging, and may even have been net up on the day.

15:21 Not training new models is actually more profitable
Levine offers a counterintuitive business logic: model capability is now ahead of deployment in many domains, and Anthropic and OpenAI are working with private equity firms to push AI into enterprises. If they stopped model development for a year, they could make a lot of money selling existing models, with quite good unit economics. But competitive pressure forces every frontier lab to keep burning huge sums training the next model — both to win customers on the leaderboards and to win researchers, because researchers want to go to the best lab. So "slowing down" is good for business, but no one dares unilaterally lay down the weapon.

19:25 Four labs sitting down to talk deceleration is collusion
Since no one dares slow down unilaterally, could the four frontier labs sit down and reach an agreement? Levine says that is legally a classic antitrust conspiracy — like the case in which BlackRock was sued by several state attorneys general: ESG investors got coal companies to produce less coal on the grounds that global warming is bad for humanity, but the effect was higher coal prices, making them the OPEC of coal. The line in the ruling is "wanting to save the world is no excuse for an antitrust conspiracy." Dario's memo also added a footnote saying antitrust law would need to be appropriately amended before they would be allowed to sit in a room and discuss shutting down the killer robots.

22:28 The founding documents are all handwritten by humans
Sylvia read Kevin Roos's book on the AGI race (out October 6; she had a pre-read copy) and found a contrast: every dramatic turning point in the book corresponds to a human handwritten memo — Dario's Pacing the Frontier, the Say AGI memo, and so on. And yet what everyone discusses now is "was this written by AI." Reading Dario's memo, she instinctively wondered "was this written by Claude," and concluded it does not read like AI at all — these people are philosophers, writing original founding texts. But the next generation will probably just ask Claude what to do.

27:31 401k has no funding gap, only a balance that is too low
A pension is a future cash flow the company has promised, and the company must invest to match that liability; invest wrong and you get a funding gap, which is why ERISA steps in to regulate pension insolvency. A 401k is not a promised cash flow, just a pool of money: if stocks fall, they fall, and there is no such thing on the books as a "billion-dollar funding gap," only "the number in your account is lower than you want." This eliminates concentration risk — with a 401k, pension insolvency can never happen. The cost is that risk shifts from the company to the individual.

30:37 Pensions were actually a great client for Wall Street
The popular story is that the shift from pensions to 401ks was good for Wall Street, because it turned people who would have retired on a pension into retail clients trading their own accounts. Levine pushes back: pensions themselves were excellent clients for Wall Street, because their long time horizon let them make the spicy investments retail would never touch — private equity, private credit. And over these decades the 401k became cheap index funds, with retail paying extremely low fees. So now the financial industry is pushing to "revive the pension," stuffing private assets into retirement accounts, because you cannot make money charging one basis point on a public stock index.

32:44 Retail says long-term, but its hands want liquidity
Private credit BDCs raise money from retail on the logic that "you have a 30-year horizon, you don't need liquidity, you should take the liquidity premium." Then this year software companies delivered bad news, investors rushed to redeem, and the BDCs could only say that each quarter just 5% of people would be allowed to redeem. Levine calls it "psychological liquidity mismatch": the fund really is making long-term investments and really should not sell long-term assets to meet redemptions; but retail psychologically wants more liquidity than the fund offers. In theory selling private assets to retirement savers is right; in practice it is very hard.

item.title: Hard Tech Is One-Fifth of the YC Batch: Software Companies Are Being Eaten by Agents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ycsp-硬科技占-yc-批次两成-软件公司正在被智能体吃掉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ycsp-硬科技占-yc-批次两成-软件公司正在被智能体吃掉/
item.description: In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the job done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.
item.content:encoded:
In YC's latest batch, hard tech companies went from 8% to 20%, with robotics, defense, semiconductors and power all doubling or more; meanwhile software companies are shifting from selling tools to selling "getting the job done," and median revenue rose from 8K to 20K.

This episode is an insider using batch data to explain trends, with concrete numbers and cases on both the hard tech and agent lines. High information density, good for quickly calibrating your judgment.

1:04 Hard tech went from 8% to 20%
Diana analyzed companies YC admitted over the last 18 to 12 months: hard tech's share went from 8% to 20%. Broken out: robotics from 1% to 6-7%, industrial manufacturing from 4% to 10%, defense from 1.5% to 5%, semiconductors and photonics from 1% to nearly 4%, power infrastructure from 1% to nearly 3%. Across the physical atom stack these numbers generally tripled to quintupled. Over the same period, the median YC company had zero revenue when admitted; in past batches median monthly revenue was about 8K by the end of the batch, and now it's 20K.

3:04 The share of technical founders is rising
Jared mentioned that in the current summer batch, one in every six founders has a PhD, far above historical levels. The reason is that working on things like silicon photonics usually requires a strong research background. Gary added that hard tech used to be hard because supply chains and software engineering were the limiting factors; now with codegen, top-tier full-stack hardware no longer requires hiring a thousand excellent engineers — one or two people, or a small team, is enough, and that changes the economics. The real bull case isn't that investors are avoiding software, but that the models themselves are accelerating scientific research, letting startups make research breakthroughs earlier.

5:05 Defense and space have become the new narrative
Gary said three macro trends are driving atom growth. First, after SpaceX's successful IPO, a generation of founders wants to build space companies, like Exosat doing sovereign Starlink solutions and Beyond Reach Labs doing satellite solar panels. Second, this generation of founders grew up in an environment where war was heavily discussed, and they want to do defense. Icarus is building a solar-powered U-2 reconnaissance aircraft that can do surveillance and communications, and has already landed a seven-figure contract with the new Department of War; Nine Mothers does counter-drone defense, a shotgun turret with CV, and special forces are procuring it. Third, compute itself is a heavily physical process: the cost of an A100 per hour is rising because demand is too great and supply too short.

8:08 Hardware companies are running at software growth rates
Nox Metals is bringing metal manufacturing back to the US, rebuilding the metal supply chain in empty Detroit factories. Its customers are emerging defense tech companies that need metal to build things, and existing suppliers are mostly slow-moving old businesses that can't keep up with the pace of new defense companies. Gary analogized to the early Web 2.0 era: new startups prefer to buy from new startups because they can collaborate at the same speed, like using Stripe instead of traditional credit card providers. PG tweeted that Nox Metals is growing at software growth rates.

10:12 The compute stack digs from chips down to power
Diana said GPU prices are anomalous: the A100 is already old, yet its cost per hour is still rising because demand exceeds supply. Around data center bring-up — site selection and construction, software, the actual buildout, power supply solutions — there are startups working at every layer. Further down to core compute silicon: Lamb Labs is building a new processor, Bot is building a new custom hardware architecture using ternary representation, because as Nvidia went from A100 to H100 to B300, floating-point precision dropped generation by generation, and LLM architectures don't need full-precision floating point — even FP2 can work. Dipole Labs is building all-optical switches, because electronic switches can't keep up with GPUs and have become the bottleneck in many data centers.

17:16 Systems of record either get eaten or become the harness
Gary proposed: if you're a system of record company, you either get raided — once you release an MCP, the data moat disappears and switching becomes easy — or you become the harness yourself, the place where people don't just read and write but get work done. He cited the RKGI benchmark as an example: the same model plugged into different harnesses performs differently, and model plus harness is what equals output. Some claim Astra with a custom harness exceeds 90% on RKGI 3, when a few months ago that number was in the low double digits.

18:19 The share of software doing complete tasks has doubled
Diana said the share of YC-admitted companies doing full-stack end-to-end tasks went from 10% to over 25%. The difference is that agents actually do the work, rather than being point solutions that still need a human to operate them, like SaaS five to eight years ago. The fastest-growing companies are exactly these doing complete workflows, such as insurance brokerage, clinical intake, medical billing. Jared added that it's been nearly a year since agentic coding became truly usable (Opus 4.5), and these workflows are now blooming across the board; people are willing to pay more for software that "gets the job done."

21:19 From zero to seven-figure revenue in three months
Diana said that this year, for the first time, she saw companies go from zero to seven-figure revenue during the batch, over a span of only three months, where this used to take 18 months or more. Part of the reason is that they're solving real problems, plus agentic coding raises product maturity, and founders can run 20 coding agent sessions at once. Another fast-growing category is selling data or RL environments to labs, and many of these companies keep a low profile. Over the past two years YC has invested in more than a dozen companies with annual revenue over $10 million selling data or RL environments, many reaching hundreds of millions of dollars, with the companies only a few years old.

item.title: The sweetest thing may not be sugar, but a beam of light shining into the brain
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-radiolab-最甜的东西可能不是糖-而是照进脑子的一束光/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-radiolab-最甜的东西可能不是糖-而是照进脑子的一束光/
item.description: Ranked by sweetness potency, sugar is not the sweetest; but by the sweetness you actually taste, sugar is nearly impossible to surpass. More disruptive still: shine a laser directly on sweet neurons, and in principle you could create a sweetness humans have never tasted.
item.content:encoded:
Ranked by sweetness potency, sugar is not the sweetest; but by the sweetness you actually taste, sugar is nearly impossible to surpass. More disruptive still: shine a laser directly on sweet neurons, and in principle you could create a sweetness humans have never tasted.

Medium information density, but the back half has real substance: only one kind of sweet receptor versus twenty to thirty bitter receptors, and using optogenetics to manufacture sweetness directly. Good for a commute listen.

4:05 The number one spot on the sweetness leaderboard is not sugar
The food industry really does rank sweet molecules, with sucrose as the benchmark. Honey is about 1.5 times sucrose, aspartame about 200 times, the katemfe fruit of the West African rainforest about 2000 times, advantame about 20000 times, and the top-ranked lugduname about 300000 times — a pinch of it can sweeten an entire swimming pool. But Eric Walters says this ranking measures only potency, meaning ‘how little of a thing it takes to light up the sweet receptor’. That is useful to soda and chewing gum makers, and it is a different question from ‘how sweet does it actually taste’.

8:25 Something 20000 times sweeter, and a kid spits it out
Latif gave his own child the number-two-ranked advantame, and the kid spat it straight onto the floor and scraped his tongue with his fingers. Scientists say it is 20000 times sweeter than sugar, yet it does not taste sweet. The reason: there is only one kind of sweet receptor, but twenty to thirty kinds of bitter receptors, so building a molecule that triggers sweetness without touching any bitter receptor is like tiptoeing through a minefield. That is why so many sugar substitutes carry off-flavors.

10:30 The sweet receptor is a dimmer, not a switch
Paul Breslin of Rutgers says that if you keep adding advantame to water, sweetness does not keep climbing to the moon — it plateaus. The sweet receptor is less like a switch and more like a dimmer: it can get brighter and brighter, but a sugar substitute can only brighten it so far. By the standard of ‘how far you can turn the dimmer up’, Eric Walters says sugar may be the sweetest thing there is — he has never tasted anything sweeter than sugar. The episode goes all the way around and comes back to the starting point, but for a deep reason: glucose is the brain's best fuel, and the sweet receptor evolved for sugar in the first place.

14:39 Strawberries taste sweeter than blueberries, but blueberries have more sugar
Blueberries actually contain twice the sugar of strawberries, yet strawberries taste sweeter. The mechanism is volatiles: strawberries release sugar-free scent molecules that get pumped from the back of the mouth into the nasal cavity as you chew and swallow, and these olfactory signals overlap with taste signals in the brain, giving sweetness a boost. Vision works the same way — dye the same sugar red, or shape it to look like fruit, and perceived sweetness rises. Latif ran the experiment live with honey plus strawberry flavoring and red coloring, and after tasting it Lulu said it was ‘noticeably sweeter’.

18:43 High notes can push sweetness up another ten percent
In research at the Science Museum in London, certain high-frequency tones raised perceived sweetness by 5% to 10%. Latif played them for Lulu, and she said it was ‘more layered, more sparkling, more crystalline’, but she also admitted this step was far subtler than the strawberry one, and that honey left sitting out crystallizes on its own, which could be a confound. Why sound affects sweetness, the episode states plainly, nobody knows for sure — it just keeps showing up in experiments.

21:50 Install bitter receptors onto the sweet pathway
Charles Zuker at Columbia University traced the entire sweet signal path from tongue to brain: tongue to ganglion, to the brainstem, to another station in the brainstem, then to the thalamus, and finally to the cortex — only at the cortex do you say ‘this is sweet’. His experimental method is direct: normally the cells carry sweet receptors, so sweetness activates this pathway; if you swap in bitter receptors there, bitter chemicals will activate the same sweet pathway. He is not doing this to find the sweetest thing, but to understand how sweetness and taste work in the brain, which might help with addiction, obesity, eating disorders and diabetes.

22:50 Use a laser to make a mouse taste a sweetness that isn't there
Zuker's team implanted a light switch into only the sweet-sensing neurons of mice, then inserted a fiber optic cable into their heads; turn on the laser and those neurons fire, and the brain says ‘sweet’ — even though the animal is eating nothing. Latif pressed him: could you crank the laser to maximum and create a sweetness humans have never tasted? Zuker said that in principle it is imaginable, that you might create the sweetest sweet, that the sweetest thing could be light. Lulu's reaction was resistance: this amounts to stripping pleasure out of the real world entirely, to the point where you would not even need to leave the house.

25:52 The kind of sugar in raspberries drifts in interstellar dust
A research team at the Center for Astrobiology in Spain observed a cloud of interstellar dust and gas near the center of the Milky Way, read its composition with spectroscopy, and found large amounts of erythrulose — a four-carbon sugar. It was the first time humans had found sugar in deep space, and a relatively complex sugar at that. As it happens, erythrulose also exists in raspberries. Latif joked that maybe somewhere there really is a space raspberry. This segment pushes ‘the sweetest thing’ from the tongue out to the cosmic scale.

item.title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as Savings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-zhixing-公积金新规-能取则取-但别把它当存款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-zhixing-公积金新规-能取则取-但别把它当存款/
item.description: The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at any time — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take is still money you should take.
item.content:encoded:
The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at any time — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take is still money you should take.

Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, and a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the public sector, is especially informative.

13:10 Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
After Zhou Yi turned on Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran out at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, which only added friction to daily life. Once she confirmed the fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai points out this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can and use everything you can’, and two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian cautions that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine for themselves — people just keep fake books for themselves.

21:12 The provident fund is not savings; not being able to withdraw is the norm
Yubai walks through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the provident fund, but the home is owner-occupied, so it qualifies neither as a home purchase nor as renting; even if the new rules allow withdrawal under the names of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs there is nothing to be done. If you risk it and invent a pretext for fraudulent withdrawal, you will be pursued to return the entire withdrawn amount and barred from withdrawing any provident fund for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate higher than a demand deposit’ — and the key is the individual's situation.

23:43 The new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list
This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying property fees on an owner-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the fund no longer serves only the single purpose of a mortgage for buying a home. Second, renting used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal scope. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management centre should respond to a withdrawal application within three days and to a loan application within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being advanced.

30:18 The share of provident fund money lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
The figure Lao Qian saw: of the money contributed to the provident fund this year, the share lent out is as low as just over 30%, while at the peak it was over 70% — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy a home is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules point toward housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation can both be withdrawn, thresholds are sharply lowered — supporting measures for a real estate market shifting from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the ageing trend: the monthly uptick in the withdrawal ratio came in 2023, exactly matching the retirement of the 1960s cohort.

32:20 If you want to buy a home, be careful about withdrawing
Yubai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou also has multiple caps; at application the smallest of several standards applies, for example a minimum 20% down payment for a first or second owner-occupied home means a 1 million yuan home can't be financed above 800,000 yuan; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income also fails. So before withdrawing the provident fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yubai is also cautious about the buying logic of ‘the rental yield is close to the provident fund rate, you're only short a down payment’: you still have to consider depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 yuan down payment is locked up.

44:05 Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
For flexible-employment workers the contribution base and rate are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The contribution base must be self-declared: below 10,000 yuan no proof is needed; above 10,000 yuan you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: 10,000 yuan at 10% to 24% is 1000 to 2400 yuan, and this money is not counted toward individual income tax, but it's a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a provident fund loan, and most do not allow a one-time catch-up payment.

47:33 In the public sector, the provident fund is an invisible benefit
Zhou Yi asked a friend back home with a public-institution post, who readily showed a screenshot of the provident fund account: the monthly deposit is more than twice hers, and the balance already exceeds her savings; the friend lives at home with no rental need, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus a supplementary occupational annuity, with the contribution base counting bonuses and allowances in full. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, and on top of that individual pension contributions are capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, so the public sector already has an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the average annual wage of urban non-private sector employees nationwide was 129,441 yuan, versus 71,590 yuan in the private sector — while working hours run the other way.

52:44 Full provident fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ has not changed at all: a company that contributes the full amount shows it respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run in every respect, rather than finding workarounds for every policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximisation the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi has run the numbers: on a wage base of 100, take-home is just over 70, but the boss pays over 130, and everyone along the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's pay raise on the Model T — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't because the capitalist had a conscience, but because the utility function worked out better that way.
