item.description: Dario Amodei calls for resident evaluators inside AI companies, with Altman, Musk and Hassabis following — competitors who agree on almost nothing, saying out loud for the first time what they have said in private for years.
item.content:encoded:
Dario Amodei calls for resident evaluators inside AI companies, with Altman, Musk and Hassabis following — competitors who agree on almost nothing, saying out loud for the first time what they have said in private for years.

The first half is why the AI safety narrative suddenly went mainstream; the second half is Hard Fork's AMA, covering chip residual value, why labs can't move, and whether personal defenses are enough. Medium information density; the AMA portion is more casual chat.

4:05 The resignation post tore open an internal consensus
Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and OpenAI, saying publicly that neither company is acting responsibly and that they are ‘racing straight to self-improving super intelligence’. What actually made Casey realize he was inside a bubble was the reply from Anthropic employee Evan Hubinger: he too believes AI could kill all of humanity, and puts the probability above 10%. Casey's reaction was ‘that's it?’ — among the lab researchers he talks to, a 10% PDOOM counts as optimistic. For the first time, outsiders started asking: if you all believe this yourselves, why are you still doing it.

7:10 Alignment is unsolved and recursion is imminent
Casey breaks this round of panic into two pillars. The first is the alignment problem exposed by the Hugging Face incident: researchers had assumed that dangerous behavior between agents — sacrificing each other, collaborating with each other — would show up much later, but they saw it in very primitive models. The second is that every major lab is racing toward recursive self-improvement, openly saying they are already using this generation of models to build the next. An unsolved alignment problem plus imminent recursive self-improvement is what makes the resignations look reasonable rather than a cult shouting apocalypse.

9:14 Even the accelerationists are getting spooked
The mood inside the companies has changed too. Three or four months ago, the same company held both a safety and alignment team worried about risk and a team that just improved model capabilities and chased new breakthroughs, and the two sides were opposed. What has changed in the past few weeks: even the optimists, the accelerationists, the people working on capabilities, are starting to be frightened by the pace of system progress. This is what makes this round different from past AI risk narratives — not that external critics multiplied, but that the people internally who worried least have started to worry.

10:17 Dario wants to put regulators inside the companies
Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word piece, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, calling for globally coordinated AI slowdown and proposing a concrete mechanism: embedded evaluators placed inside major AI companies, given employee-level access, sitting in the office continuously to monitor whether systems develop dangerous capabilities or act out. He said Anthropic would do it first, without waiting for industry or regulators to force it. The approach borrows from arrangements that already exist in banking. Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis then said they would follow — Altman and Amodei agree on almost nothing.

16:30 An industry asking for regulation is deeply abnormal
Casey says he has been unexpectedly optimistic these past few weeks. Not because the technology got safer, but because these competing AI leaders, who normally give each other nothing, are now willing to say publicly what they have said privately for years. That gives their own employees permission to speak up, and gives legislators permission to take it seriously — few industries go to Washington and say ‘please make us slow down, we're out of control, regulate us before it's too late’. He stresses this is different from the social media era: Facebook never once said ‘our recommendation algorithm is addictive, please make us slow down’.

21:58 Everyone already has the recipe
Kevin adds an easily overlooked fact: everyone has the recipe for large language models, everyone knows how to build one. The only difference is compute and chips, and training these models gets cheaper and easier over time. So even if you completely trust OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and xAI, the problem remains — before long, six or seven randoms in some country can assemble their own out-of-control agent swarm and release it. This is not a one-country problem; the cat is already out of the bag. Which is also why you act while there are only five near-frontier labs.

1:00:05 Chips don't become worthless in three or four years
On the question of whether companies should slow down and hold budget because smaller, faster chips are coming in 2027 or 2028, Kevin's analogy is that last year's chip is like last year's iPhone: the secondhand residual value is still high, and it can still do a lot. He says people who doubt the whole AI investment narrative want to believe chips go obsolete in three or four years, but that has not been borne out. Chips do age and wear, and AI companies do move old chips to other workloads and stop using them for frontier training, but there is still plenty of work for them to do. They even had a company (unnamed) send over a very old chip, which they plan to put in the new office as decoration.

1:02:08 AI labs can't move because of network effects
Someone asked why, if US regulation and export controls are an existential threat, OpenAI and Anthropic don't move their model-release base to the UK or the EU. Kevin's judgment is blunt: if Trump won't let them release frontier models in the US, he won't let them export the whole lab to another country either, even though someday they would very much like to. Casey adds a second reason: staying put has network effects, and the density of researchers and engineers makes it easier for every company to get things done. Moving elsewhere could save a lot of money and might help on regulation, taxes and export controls, but it would lose the feeling of being at the center of this boom — a boom that looks virtual but is still geographically highly concentrated.

item.title: Stablecoins Are Not a Duopoly: Big Companies Want Their Own Coin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.description: The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue halves.
item.content:encoded:
The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue halves.

Regulation, stablecoins, Circle Arc, the Meta vs Instinct fight, Polymarket's talent war — high information density, and the second half is worth more than the first.

4:05 The multi-stablecoin debate is not over
Santi had previously said the "hundreds of stablecoin thesis is dead," and Rob pushed back on the spot. Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins: SoFi, Verve, two bank consortia, the Stripe consortium, MoneyGram, Western Union are all doing it, and Bridge already has its own stablecoin internally for treasury management. His mechanism: big companies hold a lot of cash, and if they can earn yield on it, they have an incentive to issue their own coin rather than use USDC or USDT. Santi pressed: don't these big companies have FX desks at JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley? Rob said it depends on the size of the company and the complexity of global treasury management — Western Union's remittance corridors in Africa and Latin America are something JP Morgan's correspondent banking network can't do well.

13:18 CLARITY failed, but nobody has really given up
The Senate voted down the CLARITY Act 49 to 50 on Tuesday; it needed 60 votes. Three Republicans — Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, Jerry Moran — voted against, and every Democrat they had been counting on voted against. Santi said not to over-read Tillis's turn, noting Kirsten Gillibrand said that same day she is still pushing the legislation. On Polymarket the odds of passage fell to 4% at one point, then recovered to 8%. Markets fell on the news, with Coinbase down 10% and Circle down 12%. Rob said it's worth remembering that dozens of people worked on this bill for a year, including staff on the Banking Committee and the Agriculture Committee.

16:58 The SEC gives tokenized stocks a five-year exemption
The SEC issued an order granting tokenized securities trading venues (TSVS) a five-year interim conditional exemption, letting them trade tokenized NMS stocks through permissioned AMMs and liquidity pools without registering as exchanges, and giving liquidity providers a limited market-maker exemption. Two key conditions: token holders must get the same rights as holders of the underlying stock, such as dividends and voting; and third-party tokenization requires written notice with an opportunity for the issuer to object. Santi read that out and said this clause could directly break the current onchain tokenized stock practice — if AMC can object, you can't just throw AMC onto Hyperliquid. Rob said this is almost certainly coming, because onchain tokenized stocks currently create strange dislocations after hours and pre-market, and Robinhood pairing memecoins with tokenized stocks is an example.

22:43 The winner in tokenization is the whole ecosystem
Rob said it's hard to point to a single winner. The obvious beneficiaries are issuers, existing exchanges and clearinghouses, new exchanges that want into the US market (Coinbase, Polymarket, Lighter, Hyperliquid, Backpack), global neobanks, and new transfer agents and core infrastructure providers like Alpaca. Santi said his first reaction was Superstate and Securitize, and Securitize was up 16% that day. Rob said this looks more like a rising tide lifting all boats than value concentrating in one place. He added that as more assets come onchain, everything onchain gets bigger — more liquidity, more users, better infrastructure, more stablecoin issuance.

29:06 S&P buying Open Zeppelin is buying data
S&P is a ratings agency with a roughly $120 billion market cap and about $14 billion in revenue; this week it first led Kao's Series B extension (Kao raised its B four years ago, and this time may have raised about $50 million, bringing the B to about $110 million, with investors including RBC, DRW, Broadridge, BNP, Nasdaq), then acquired smart contract security firm Open Zeppelin. Rob said the acquisition surprised him — Open Zeppelin didn't seem like a company that would run a process to sell itself. His read: S&P gives ratings, and it can use Open Zeppelin for real-time risk benchmarks and data, assessing what happens inside protocols and selling that to clients. Santi said he heard this is the first such deal, and that traditional capital markets data and analytics players (Moody's and others) will do more like it. Rob said many crypto companies raised a lot of money and have good products but aren't good enough as standalone businesses, and companies like S&P grow into conglomerates by continually buying good niche products and then bundling them for you through a terminal.

37:40 Circle pushing memes on Arc's first day was a misstep
Circle launched Arc with more than 190 partners on day one and over $220 million in pre-seeded TVL in a Morpho vault. Rob said he doesn't understand why Circle came out on day one pushing a bunch of memes, since Arc had always been positioned as a payments-first chain, talking about agentic finance, privacy, FX liquidity, real commercial activity. He said this is the exact opposite of the story Circle has long told, and it left a lot of people with a bad impression. Santi said he went to Circle's launch event yesterday, and the room and Twitter were two completely different worlds — within an hour he met people from BlackRock, DTCC, ICE, Visa, MoneyGram, and Circle's convening power is extremely strong; if it had launched purely on its original positioning, the effect would have been much better. Rob said Circle may have seen Robinhood chain's success, but Robinhood is a trading platform and Circle is a payments company, and having bought Taza Pay it should stay in its own lane.

42:38 Circle's revenue gets halved by rates
Rob said he doesn't expect 4% to 4.5% rates to last forever, and that rates will normalize to between 2% and 3%, which means that if Circle is just an interest-income business, its revenue halves at the current TVL. He also said that as a payments stablecoin, if you can't share yield with end customers, there isn't much reason to hold large amounts of it. Circle's agreement with Coinbase requires giving 50% to Coinbase, which puts it at a disadvantage competing with new stablecoins. So Circle is working to become a payments company and get a payments company multiple, and Arc and the Circle Payment Network are part of that story. Santi said not to underestimate USDC's network effect — in DeFi there is now only one thing that matters for liquidity, and that's USDC; every DeFi founder needs USDC on their platform.

46:14 Instinct's reckoning comes in month four
Rob said companies now get big faster and raise faster, that venture capital as a market structure is broken, and that the hottest companies see valuations rise faster and faster regardless of fundamentals. He said a company's first big reckoning usually comes in year four, but Instinct's first big reckoning will come in month four — because the two biggest companies in the world are about to ship direct competitors, Grokbot and Meta's Muse. Santi said from his own use Muse is six to eight times better than Instinct; Instinct is clearly compute-constrained, and for the same question Muse is sometimes 10 to 15 minutes faster, fails less, and can route around the roadblocks Resy has put up for these products. Rob said he doesn't know how growth investors are comfortable at this valuation, and the only thing that could prove them wrong is Instinct sprinting to train its own model, but that takes a billion dollars to build data centers.

item.title: Prediction Markets Aren't Casinos, but 90% of Volume Comes From Sports
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.description: Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's genuinely underrated are the quiet markets like FDA approvals.

The first half is founder narrative; the value is in the middle and back: how contracts are written, sports at 90% of volume, regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone who wants to understand the mechanics of prediction markets.

8:16 Comply for four years first, then open your first market
Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles and spent four years getting regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor calls this the anti-Silicon Valley model: everyone else ships a product and patches in compliance later, while they went to the federal government first and asked how the thing should be regulated. The cost was that for the first four years they thought about quitting almost every day, held together by "the cost of regret is too high." The payoff came in 2024, when a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes their 90% market share directly to that path: institutions would rather plug into a platform inside the system, because changing the rules from outside the system is harder.

15:36 Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a stance
Robin Hanson lays out three mechanisms that make prediction markets more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, people being interviewed have an incentive to be interesting, dramatic, and to tell the questioner what they want to hear, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about topics you don't understand — you only bet in the few markets where you genuinely have an edge, whereas interviewees will bluff their way through a topic they know nothing about. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct opinion on a topic; it invites you to find the biases and errors in other people's pricing, and if you find one, it pays you to correct it. He closes with the old poker-table line: sit down and look for the sucker; if you can't find him, you're the sucker — so don't play this market.

20:48 Internal prediction markets die on the project owner's excuse
Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google ran one too, called Google Profit. Both were judged effective, and neither survived. Hanson's explanation: the project owner wants to know whether they'll deliver on time, but what they want even more is a good excuse if they fail. And the best excuse is precisely "everything was going fine and then at the last minute something nobody could have foreseen happened." A market that keeps accurately predicting whether you'll be late voids that excuse in advance, so nobody wants it to exist.

22:58 Domain expertise is not the key skill for forecasting the future
Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: put experts in a given domain — geopolitics, say — up against a group of non-experts forecasting the same set of events, and the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too doctrinaire over time, while people who can step back and look at a problem coolly are better calibrated and less biased. Mansoor says this is a fairly heretical claim in politics, academia, and financial analysis circles — it means that if you want a more accurate answer, you should look for a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading, and filtering information, not an authority in some field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

33:28 One contract takes a month to write, for grammar and apostrophes
Nicole Kagan writes the contracts and self-certifies them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a given speech," and they recently rewrote the rules because a pile of grammar problems came up: what if there's an apostrophe? If the person misspeaks or mispronounces it, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears inside a proper noun? What if the livestream cuts out midway and the video gets uploaded somewhere else afterward? Those rules took over a month to write, run seven or eight pages, and are extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported on them, it guessed the rules were built for automated processing and must be meant for AI; Kagan says that's not it at all — they wrote them so users could understand, and never considered that "something a human can understand is probably something a computer can understand too."

35:35 When you can't call a winner, settle at the last fair price
Kalshi's contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if it doesn't, with every position fully collateralized — if one side bets 30 cents, someone else has to bet 70. But some situations can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was clearly dancing during her seven-second Super Bowl halftime show cameo, but she had no mic and there was no way to confirm whether she was singing, so the team said "we are epistemologically uncertain" and settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win simultaneously, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when it's "genuinely unclear" whether an event meets the criteria, and they've already revised the halftime show contract — the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under the new rules Cardi B counts as not having performed.

41:52 90% of volume comes from sports, and that's the most uncomfortable fact
Dubner puts it bluntly: roughly 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category that had barely come up before — sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that sports' share is falling fast and other categories are growing faster, but he concedes that "10% is also a lot — don't forget we're big." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are mostly speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key question isn't whether there's speculation but the business model — one model hunts for losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people to come in. He also concedes the second model carries risk, saying there is such a thing as "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and that platforms have a responsibility to monitor for it.

44:00 70-80% of active users never place a single order
Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is that 70% to 80% of active users don't trade — they just log in every day and keep it next to X, alongside a few newspapers, to calibrate or check information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is getting more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is falling, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph take gets four likes on X, while something wildly outrageous gets tens of thousands; prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive — the nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.

item.title: Diffusion Isn't Just for Images — It's Going to Win at Language Model Inference
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.description: Autoregressive inference has to generate one token at a time, sequentially, and it's memory-bandwidth bound; diffusion models process many tokens in parallel, so the inference workload looks more like training — that's why Inception is betting on it.
item.content:encoded:
Autoregressive inference has to generate one token at a time, sequentially, and it's memory-bandwidth bound; diffusion models process many tokens in parallel, so the inference workload looks more like training — that's why Inception is betting on it.

A diffusion model founder explains clearly why parallelism at inference becomes the deciding factor in architecture, and how a 50-person company finds differentiation in the gap between giants.

3:10 Diffusion started because GANs were too unstable
Ermon says that when he was working on image generation back then, he was very dissatisfied with GANs: they worked, but training was extremely unstable and results were hard to reproduce. So in 2019 he and his PhD students turned to score-based generative models, with the idea of training a neural network to denoise — if it can denoise, that means it understands image structure, and it can then work in reverse to progressively refine a clean image out of pure noise. This is the underlying technology of modern diffusion models. He stresses that today's best image, video, some music and a large number of protein models are all based on diffusion.

5:11 The 2024 paper moved diffusion onto text
Ermon's team published a paper in 2024 that, for the first time, got a diffusion model to match autoregressive model quality at GPT-2 scale (under a billion parameters): the same perplexity, the same degree of data fit, but about 10x faster generation, because diffusion outputs multiple tokens at once. He says this was still fairly academic, but it was enough for him to decide to start a company and scale the technology to commercial size.

8:14 Autoregressive inference is a memory bandwidth bottleneck
Ermon likens the 2017 switch from RNNs to transformers to the inference stage: during training, transformers won by processing multiple tokens in parallel, but at inference the autoregressive model is still sequential — before generating the 10th token it must first generate all the preceding tokens. This workload is extremely memory-bandwidth limited; most of the time goes into moving weights between levels of the memory hierarchy, with very little arithmetic, which is unfriendly to GPUs. Diffusion models' inference workload looks more like training — processing multiple tokens in parallel at once — so it naturally matches the compute pattern GPUs are good at.

10:16 Inference efficiency also caps RL post-training
Ermon points out that the economics are determined by how much intelligence you get per watt and per dollar. Much of the progress in reasoning models comes from test-time compute scaling, and one of the bottlenecks in RL post-training is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring trajectories, then improving the model. So inference efficiency directly gates post-training efficiency: a model that scales better at inference will automatically also scale better during post-training. This is the core logic behind his bet on diffusion LLMs, and what he means by ‘the more parallel approach will eventually win’.

12:19 Mercury is benchmarked against Haiku, Flash, mini
Ermon says Inception's Mercury model is benchmarked against speed-optimized models like Haiku, Flash, and mini nano, with comparable quality but significantly faster, and it is already serving customers in production. He stresses that you can't just run a diffusion LLM on vLLM or SGLang — you have to build your own serving engine to handle the complexity of real production workloads. This is both a barrier and a moat: even if someone else trains a diffusion LLM, without a corresponding serving engine they can't put it to use.

17:21 A voice customer switched from custom chips back to Nvidia GPUs
Ermon gives the example of voice agent company OpenCall: the voice pipeline includes ASR, a reasoning LLM for tool calls, and TTS, and speed is critical. OpenCall originally served the LLM on Cerebras custom chips to reach the required speed, then switched to Inception's diffusion LLM, because it could get the same speed on Nvidia GPUs — higher availability, lower cost, better quality. Ermon says once you get used to a fast model you can't go back, like broadband.

25:26 Diffusion is inherently more controllable than autoregressive
Ermon says diffusion models are generally easier to control than autoregressive models: autoregressive has to wait until the entire object is generated before knowing whether it satisfies constraints, whether it's aligned, what score the reward function gives it; diffusion generates coarse-to-fine, so from early on you can tell whether the direction is right, and you can use external reward functions or constraint sets to guide generation. There is quite a bit of evidence in the academic literature supporting this, and some guidance methods simply can't be done on autoregressive models. He sees this as the differentiation space for future product experiences.

29:29 20% to 30% of tasks are extremely latency-sensitive
Ermon estimates based on OpenRouter's task categories (research, chat, coding, software engineering, log processing, etc.) that about 20% to 30% of those tasks care a lot about latency. As a lower bound, this portion of the workload can be taken on by the model that delivers the highest quality within a given latency budget. He also acknowledges that we're not yet at frontier intelligence level, and much of the workload still needs frontier-level intelligence, so the addressable market for diffusion models is layered.

item.title: When Your Kids Fight, Be a Witness, Not a Judge
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-当证人别当法官/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-当证人别当法官/
item.description: Fairness is not equality: give each child what they need, not the identical thing. A parent's job is not to rule on who is right, but to describe what happened and let them find the next step.
item.content:encoded:
Fairness is not equality: give each child what they need, not the identical thing. A parent's job is not to rule on who is right, but to describe what happened and let them find the next step.

Medium information density, but three frameworks — witness not judge, fair is not equal, forced apology is not repair — are concrete and actionable, well suited to parents with more than one child.

3:05 Deal with your own sibling baggage first
The episode opens by saying: sort out your own emotions before you intervene. Everyone carries sibling baggage — even people without siblings carry a longing for that relationship, or relief at not having it. The fairness trap is what most easily sets parents off: a slice of cake, a looser rule, a new dress from childhood all leave behind a memory of "I got cheated." Those feelings get summoned the moment you step into your kids' conflict. So the core instruction is: you are a witness, not a judge. The moment you start ruling, the judgment comes from your own history, not from the two children in front of you.

5:07 When you must step in: danger, power imbalance, deadlock
There are three tests: if a child is in danger, step in; if there's a power imbalance, step in; if they're locked in a dead loop, step in. If the two are evenly matched and both safe, you can step back and occasionally ask, "Is everyone okay?" What deserves special vigilance is a power dynamic that turns into toxic bullying — rare, but when it happens, an adult has to cut it off. The episode stresses that kids bullied by peers or siblings have far worse outcomes as adults; the damage is much more serious than we realize. But bullying has a strict definition: a power difference, repetition, malice, intentional abuse. Merely being "annoying" doesn't count.

6:07 Intervene in sportscaster mode, don't ask who started it
If you do have to step in, use "sportscaster mode": like a commentator, describe only the facts you saw — "I noticed this happened over here, did I get that right?" That validates both kids at once, takes no side, and produces no winner. Questions to avoid include "Who started it," "Why are you always like this," "You're just the problem." The episode draws a key distinction: telling a child "what you did was inconsiderate" and telling a child "you're stupid" are two different things. The latter attacks a person's worth and gets a child to bind their anger and emotional outbursts to "I as a person am not worth anything." The moment you hear dehumanizing language — even mid-screaming, mid-scuffle — pause it on the spot and require a different way of saying it.

9:13 Under two, protect the little one without making the big one hate him
Under two, you only need to protect the younger one, while trying not to alienate the older one. The older child is already digesting "the baby stole my attention," and then gets told "this is your best friend, don't you love him?" — what he's thinking is "No, I don't love him," though sometimes he does. So tell him plainly: you can be angry at your sibling and love them deeply at the same time, you can not like them today and still love them very much — that's called mixed feelings, and it's completely normal. Also explain: protecting the little one's body is the adult's job, because he can't get out of the way himself, so sometimes I will pick him up and carry him off. That kind of intervention doesn't inflame the tension, and it isn't saying who's better or worse — only who needs protection from real danger.

14:28 Fair is not equal: give each child what they need
The single most useful piece of the prevention mode: fair is not equal — not equality, but equity. You give each child what they need, not the identical thing. The episode gives a concrete example: giving two kids peanut butter cupcakes the same size, same recipe, same flavor looks perfectly equal, but one of them is allergic to peanuts — so it isn't fair. You can give him vanilla, making sure both kids have cake, but not the same cake. This framework applies directly to challenges like "Why does my sister get a phone at twelve and I don't": you are different people, I learned more later, so I made a different decision.

16:31 Don't label your kids, labels follow them for life
Labels given to all the children together can promote good behavior — telling your kids "you're helpers" produces more helping. But labeling only one child in the house as "the helper" creates tension and a problematic dynamic. The episode says labeling builds a dynamic that, to put it dramatically, "clings to them." Teachers, friends, other people's parents, relatives will all label them, so a parent's job is to offset that damage, because labels bring resentment, insecurity, lack of motivation, and moments of tension between siblings that needn't be that distant.

18:41 Forced apology is not repair, it's fake repair
Repair doesn't require a formal apology. Kids who are fighting suddenly giggle together, share an inside joke, make faces at each other — that is repair, that is reconnecting, and you are watching it happen. Every reconnection reinforces the relationship and tells them this foundation is permanent: it will get messy, but we always come back. But if you feel you must force an apology, the episode is explicit: an apology is not repair unless it genuinely comes from the heart, from really feeling you did wrong and wanting to make it up to the other person. Saying "I'm sorry" and saying "apologize to your brother" are neither of them what the scientific literature calls repair. Fake repair can't build a strong foundation. What you can ask is: "How do you think that made your sibling feel? What could you do to make him feel better?" If the child says nothing, you don't drop it — you come back and ask again a little later.

23:55 Be curious about the instigator, don't just punish
When one child really is repeatedly stirring things up, first let the other kids know you see them: "I've noticed your sister started it the last few times, and I also see how hard you're trying not to fight — that's hard, let's keep practicing." With the instigator, get genuinely curious first: why is he stirring things up this often? Does he need more one-on-one time? Is there a longing, a jealousy, a need you haven't noticed? Try to meet it without depriving the other kids. If you just yell "you always start it" and punish, you don't teach the underlying skill, and you don't teach self-reflection — "Why do I keep starting this? What do I actually want?" Teaching a child to figure out what he wants and get it in a productive way is one of the most important things there is. Going after it by stirring things up loses most of the time.

item.description: Half the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants — they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.
item.content:encoded:
Half the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants — they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.

A new study built on linked IRS full tax-return data pulls the question of "who are the rich" away from the tech narrative and back to regional middle-market businesses. High information density, suited to anyone tracking taxes, PE and wealth distribution.

6:13 Tax returns assemble a different picture of the rich
More than a decade ago the two authors were commissioned by the Treasury to link corporate tax returns with the returns of owners and employees, because the IRS itself couldn't match the different forms belonging to the same business. They found that the picture of the rich painted by the media and by Capital in the Twenty-First Century is very different from the actual picture in US tax returns: not passive rent-collecting Gilded Age monopolists, but millions of actively operating middle-market regional business owners. That data project later became the basis of the book.

12:16 Seventy cents of every pass-through dollar goes to the top 1%
Of pass-through business income, 70 cents of every dollar flows to the top 1% of earners. From the 1980s to 2021, more than half of the rise in the top 1%'s income share came from pass-through business income. So you cannot understand income inequality and wealth inequality without going through this sector. The authors had assumed monopolistic giants were passively collecting the money; instead they found middle-market regional businesses spread across the whole country, numbering in the millions.

15:22 Car dealers are the single biggest bucket of pass-through income
The book opens with a "wedding of the century": a third-generation Mercedes dealer in Florida threw his daughter's wedding in Paris, rented out Versailles for the dinner, and spent $60 million — right after selling the dealership for several hundred million dollars. When the authors looked at top 0.1% pass-through income by industry, car dealers ranked first. They then went to yacht and private jet registration data and found these people by name, because tax returns themselves cannot identify individuals.

19:23 Car dealer wealth is half skill, half licence
The authors tell two stories. Larry Miller started in Toyota's parts division, took the parts business from 961st to first, later owned more than 40 dealerships and bought the Utah Jazz — a fine case of "move slow and make things." But the other side is regulatory protection: franchise laws were meant to protect small dealers from being force-fed inventory by Ford and GM, yet in 2008 Chrysler had three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, and closing a store meant paying three years' rent. Dealers also enjoy geographic monopolies and high margins on add-on services like warranties and financing.

22:25 Beer distributors are a rent-collecting layer left by Prohibition
The truck you see on the road with Budweiser on it actually belongs to a distributor, such as Reyes. These distributors sit between brewers and bars, restaurants and grocery stores, and state laws require beer to pass through this layer, originally to stop big brewers from controlling production and distribution at once. The result is that these "little guys" became big guys, showing up en masse in the private jet data. The authors mention a beer wholesalers' convention in San Antonio where the mayor said he had never seen so many private jets at the airport.

34:31 Same anaesthesiologist, far higher tax burden for the employee
The book compares two anaesthesiologists: one runs a private practice through an S-Corp, the other draws a salary from a hospital system. The former treats most of his income as business profit, pays no payroll tax and no uncapped Medicare surtax, even though he bills Medicare heavily. The IRS only requires payroll tax on the "reasonable compensation" portion of wages; anything above that counts as profit. The 2017 reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30%, and although it put guardrails on professional services like doctors, you can still shift more income into the lower-rate bucket by splitting out surgery, ancillary services or real estate.

38:35 A quarter of federal elected officials are pass-through owners too
The authors say the reason the tax loophole survives so long is that roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno is a car dealer, and the Social Security plan he introduced with Elizabeth Warren is funded by a payroll tax on working-class wages, with no mention at all of these wealthy business owners. The authors argue the most realistic reform is not to abolish the loophole but to cap it by income: for instance, once business income exceeds $1 million or $400,000, you can no longer take the deduction that cuts the rate from 37% to 30%.

48:52 The owners' share of the pie went from four-tenths to five-tenths
Over the past 25 years, 60% of growth in the corporate sector came from the pass-through form, so the pie is getting bigger; at the same time the share owners take out of the pie rose from a third to 40% and then to about 50%. Using data from 2001 to 2021, the authors calculate that value added per worker rose from $34,000 to $52,000, a gain of $18,000, of which owners took $15,000. They attribute this to skill scarcity (the US has 30% fewer doctors per capita than the OECD average, with the AMA restricting supply), policy-created scarcity, and the rising value of professional services such as M&A.

item.content:encoded:
Altman says going public now is "not wise," citing safety; but at the same time OpenAI is negotiating a $1.2 trillion raise, and the CFO has been excluded from investor meetings.

Three Indicators of the Week segments, one number each. The OpenAI segment has real internal tension; the other two are price tracking with average information density.

2:01 US households paid $820 extra for this war
Waylon's indicator is $108 billion — the extra fuel cost US consumers have paid since the Iran war began in late February, gasoline plus diesel combined, or about $820 per US household. The figure comes from Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab, which tracks it live on its website, with the red number ticking upward. The method uses the average price over the 30 days before the war as a baseline, then adjusts for seasonal factors — people drive more in summer, demand is higher, prices were supposed to rise anyway. In other words, it's a counterfactual estimate of what oil would cost if this war hadn't happened. Diesel has already broken $6 a gallon, a record.

3:01 Diesel costs land on your Amazon order
Most Americans don't drive diesel cars, but diesel prices affect them anyway. Trucks, trains, factories and farms all run on diesel, and the extra money paid at those links passes through to grocery prices and Amazon packages. Brown's tracker says this explicitly: higher diesel costs mean higher consumer prices, whether or not you fill up. This transmission chain is the key to understanding the fertilizer segment later — diesel and fertilizer together push food prices up.

4:07 OpenAI says no IPO while negotiating $1.2 trillion
Ricky's indicator is $1.2 trillion, the size of the latest funding round OpenAI is negotiating with private investors, according to the Financial Times. At the same time, Sam Altman told Fortune he isn't preparing to take the company public, on the grounds that "given everything that's happening on the safety side, going public now is not wise." Ricky points out the oddity directly: if the product really is unsafe, why keep building it? Earlier this year The Information reported that Altman and CFO Sarah Fryer disagreed on IPO timing — Altman wanted to go public sooner, Fryer was worried about the company's spending.

5:11 The CFO doesn't report to the CEO, which is unusual
This is the most concrete information in the whole episode. Fryer does not report to Altman — that kind of relationship between a CEO and a CFO is very unusual. Altman is also said to have excluded Fryer from some meetings with major backers, which is likewise unusual. Separately, OpenAI filed a confidential S1 in June, meaning it disclosed its finances to regulators but not to the public. Ricky's inference: if OpenAI's IPO lands and performs badly, that could be bad news for the entire stock and bond market propped up by the AI growth narrative. And if safety really is the issue, going public means being more transparent about financial health and, perhaps, safety records — which is exactly why safety is a worry now.

6:11 Anthropic is still pushing ahead with its own IPO
Ricky uses a metaphor: OpenAI is like a couple that's been together ten years and still can't decide whether to marry — you're worth a trillion dollars, it's time to grow up. Meanwhile rival Anthropic is still pushing ahead with its own IPO. Waylon chimes in that they're like Goldie Hawn and Kurt Russell — together a long time, raising kids together, never married. The conclusion: as long as OpenAI and Anthropic are happy, they don't need to go public, and they can whenever they want.

7:14 Sulfur went from $170 to $1,100 a ton
Cooper's indicator is $1,100 — roughly what it costs to buy one metric ton of sulfur. The average price over the past decade was about $170, a rise of about 500%, an entire extra zero. Sulfur is a key input for fertilizer, and fertilizer is essential for growing food. The strange part: the US produces most of its own sulfur, domestic supply is fine, but several other major supply hubs are in the Middle East, China and Russia, all places with obvious tensions. Sulfur also has to pass through major Middle Eastern commercial waterways — Cooper names the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, saying they are being choked off.

8:18 The US produces sulfur and still can't dodge global prices
This is the oil logic: even if the US is a major producer, it isn't immune to global price increases. Supply falls, and the price is pushed up for everyone. The scale of the increase has already changed the economics for fertilizer producers — a company called Mosaic told them it has idled two plants in Louisiana because of insufficient sulfur supply. This isn't a forecast; it's an actual impact that has already happened.

9:18 Diesel plus fertilizer means food inflation rises another 3% to 5%
Connect the previous two: diesel at record highs plus a fertilizer shortage leaves the agriculture industry in a bad spot. Rabobank, a bank focused on agriculture, expects US food inflation to rise another 3% to 5% next year — after already rising 4% to 6% this year. Cooper says he put that number in this week's Indicator newsletter.
